## Introduction: why does temperature not throw the clock off? {#sec-intro}

Our body temperature, hormone secretion, and waves of sleepiness follow cycles of approximately 24 hours. Similar rhythms of roughly one day occur in the opening and closing of plant leaves, the formation of fungal spores, and even in single-celled bacteria. They are called *circadian rhythms*, from Latin words meaning "about a day."

Not every fluctuation with a period of roughly 24 hours qualifies as a circadian rhythm, however. Circadian rhythms have three recognized properties. First, they continue to oscillate with a period of about 24 hours even under constant light and temperature conditions: *self-sustained oscillation*. Organisms do not simply follow the external day–night cycle; they have an internal clock. Second, they can shift the phase of that clock to align with cycles of light and darkness or temperature: *entrainment*. Because an internal clock's period is not exactly 24 hours, it needs a small daily adjustment. Third, its period changes very little when the ambient temperature changes: *temperature compensation*.

Of these three properties, temperature compensation is the most puzzling. Chemical reaction rates depend strongly on temperature: many biological reactions become about two to three times faster for a 10 °C rise. This factor is called the temperature coefficient, Q~10~. An internal clock, too, must run through a succession of chemical reactions, such as protein binding and phosphorylation. We might therefore expect it to run faster on warm days and slower on cold ones. Yet the period Q~10~ of actual circadian rhythms generally lies between about 0.8 and 1.2.^[In this article, the period Q~10~ is defined as $\tau(T)/\tau(T+10\,^\circ\mathrm{C})$. It exceeds 1 when warming shortens the period, or speeds up the clock, so its direction agrees with the Q~10~ of an ordinary chemical reaction. Some publications use the reciprocal, $\tau(T+10\,^\circ\mathrm{C})/\tau(T)$ [@fu2024], so care is needed when comparing values.] The components are temperature-sensitive, but the clock assembled from them is not.

This seems somewhat at odds with the second property, entrainment. To entrain to a temperature cycle, a clock must be able to sense changes in temperature. To achieve temperature compensation, on the other hand, it must be insensitive to temperature. How can it sense temperature without being governed by it? We will return to this question at the end of the article.

Cyanobacteria, also known as blue-green algae, provide a particularly useful way to approach this puzzle. They are photosynthetic bacteria. In 1993, experiments using a bioluminescent reporter showed that their gene expression exhibits a circadian rhythm with a temperature-compensated period [@kondo1993]. At the heart of this clock are three proteins: KaiA, KaiB, and KaiC.

Remarkably, in 2005, mixing just these three proteins with ATP in a test tube was shown to produce an approximately daily oscillation in KaiC phosphorylation [@nakajima2005]. The periods were approximately 22, 21, and 20 hours at 25, 30, and 35 °C, respectively, giving a Q~10~ of about 1.1. A temperature-compensated clock was running without gene transcription, translation, or even a cell.

If temperature compensation occurs with just three proteins in a test tube, we can investigate its mechanism through both molecules and mathematics. This article takes a systems biology approach: understanding the clock through the behavior of an interconnected reaction network, rather than through the properties of a single molecule alone. We first review how the KaiABC clock works and express the condition for temperature compensation mathematically. We then test those equations by running a clock model in Python. Looking beyond the period to how oscillation amplitude changes with temperature, we consider three ways for a temperature-compensated clock to remain sensitive to temperature, and compare them with experimental data and measured temperature dependences of individual reactions. All code in the article can be run as written to reproduce the figures.

## How the KaiABC oscillator works {#sec-kai}

The central player, KaiC, is a ring-shaped protein made of six subunits: a hexamer. Each subunit contains two domains, CI and CII. Together, the six subunits form two stacked rings, one of CI domains and one of CII domains, with overall dimensions of roughly 10 nm (@fig-kaic (a)) [@pattanayek2004; @egli2013]. Both domains bind ATP. The hexamer binds 12 ATP molecules in total, each nestled at an interface between neighboring subunits.

KaiC can both phosphorylate and dephosphorylate itself. Phosphorylation occurs at two sites in the CII domain: serine 431 (S431) and threonine 432 (T432). A KaiC subunit can therefore occupy four states: U, with neither site phosphorylated; T, with only T432 phosphorylated; ST, with both sites phosphorylated; and S, with only S431 phosphorylated. During oscillations in vitro, these states follow a fixed order. T432 is phosphorylated first, producing T, followed by S431, producing ST. The phosphate on T432 is then removed, producing S, and finally the phosphate on S431 is removed, returning the subunit to U [@nishiwaki2007; @rust2007].

```{python}
#| label: fig-kaic
#| fig-cap: "Structure of the KaiC hexamer (PDB 1TF7) [@pattanayek2004]. (a) Side view, showing the stacked CI (blue) and CII (orange) rings. Different shades distinguish the six subunits. The blue bands along the sides of the CII ring are linkers connecting CI to CII. (b) A section through the CII ring at the height of S431 and T432, viewed from the CII side. ATP molecules bound to CII are shown intact. The first 13 N-terminal and last 22 C-terminal residues are unresolved in this crystal structure. Rendered from atomic coordinates in Python using Biopython, NumPy, and Matplotlib."
#| fig-width: 10.5
#| fig-height: 5.4
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Figure code (rendering the PDB 1TF7 atomic coordinates)"
from Bio.PDB import MMCIFParser
from matplotlib.patches import Patch

# --- Load the structure (PDB 1TF7) -------------------------------------------
CI_END = 260                     # Residues 1–260: CI, including the linker to CII
VDW = {"C": 1.7, "N": 1.55, "O": 1.52, "S": 1.8, "P": 1.8}
records = []
for chain in MMCIFParser(QUIET=True).get_structure("KaiC", "../../../posts/2026-10-16/1TF7.cif")[0]:
    for res in chain:
        het, num, _ = res.id
        if het == " ":
            kind = "phos" if num in (431, 432) else ("CI" if num <= CI_END else "CII")
        elif res.get_resname() == "ATP":
            kind = "ATP_CII" if num % 10 == 1 else "ATP_CI"   # x901: CII; x903: CI in this file
        else:
            continue                                         # Water molecules, etc.
        for atom in res:
            records.append((chain.id, kind, atom.element, num, atom.get_id(), *atom.coord))
chain_ids = sorted({r[0] for r in records})
chain_no = np.array([chain_ids.index(r[0]) for r in records])
kind = np.array([r[1] for r in records])
xyz = np.array([r[5:8] for r in records], float)
radius = np.array([VDW.get(r[2], 1.7) for r in records]) * 1.2

atom_name = np.array([r[4] for r in records])

# Distance from terminal ATP phosphorus (PG) in CII to the nearest T432 side-chain oxygen (OG1)
pg = xyz[(kind == "ATP_CII") & (atom_name == "PG")]
og1 = xyz[(kind == "phos") & (atom_name == "OG1")]
d_atp_t432 = np.linalg.norm(pg[:, None, :] - og1[None, :, :], axis=2).min(axis=1)

center = xyz.mean(axis=0)
axis = xyz[kind == "CII"].mean(axis=0) - xyz[kind == "CI"].mean(axis=0)   # Sixfold axis, from CI toward CII
axis /= np.linalg.norm(axis)
height = (xyz - center) @ axis

# --- Colors -----------------------------------------------------------------
def rgb(hexcode):
    return np.array([int(hexcode[i:i + 2], 16) for i in (1, 3, 5)]) / 255
PALETTE = {"CI": ("#a9c8ee", "#7ea9df"), "CII": ("#f6c7a8", "#eca07a"),
           "ATP": "#f2c230", "phos": "#c2255c"}
colors = np.zeros((len(records), 3)); group = np.zeros(len(records), int)
for i, (k, c) in enumerate(zip(kind, chain_no)):
    if k in ("CI", "CII"):
        colors[i] = rgb(PALETTE[k][c % 2]); group[i] = 10 * c + (1 if k == "CI" else 2)   # Alternate subunit shades
    elif k == "phos":
        colors[i] = rgb(PALETTE["phos"]); group[i] = 10 * c + 3
    else:
        colors[i] = rgb(PALETTE["ATP"]); group[i] = 100 + 10 * c + (1 if k == "ATP_CII" else 3)

# --- Render atoms as spheres with a z-buffer, shading, and outlines ----------
def view_matrix(view_dir, up):
    """Rotation matrix whose rows are screen x, y, and z (toward the viewer)."""
    z = view_dir / np.linalg.norm(view_dir)
    y = up - np.dot(up, z) * z; y /= np.linalg.norm(y)
    return np.vstack([np.cross(y, z), y, z])

def render(mask, R, px=0.22, ss=3, fog=0.35, depth_jump=5.0, line=1):
    p = (xyz[mask] - center) @ R.T
    rad, col, grp = radius[mask], colors[mask], group[mask]
    s = px / ss                                                 # Supersample, then downsample
    lo = p[:, :2].min(0) - rad.max() - 4; hi = p[:, :2].max(0) + rad.max() + 4
    W, H = np.ceil((hi - lo) / s).astype(int)
    depth = np.full((H, W), -np.inf); index = np.full((H, W), -1); nz = np.zeros((H, W))
    gx, gy = (p[:, 0] - lo[0]) / s, (hi[1] - p[:, 1]) / s
    for i in range(len(p)):
        r = rad[i] / s
        xs = np.arange(max(int(gx[i] - r), 0), min(int(gx[i] + r) + 2, W))
        ys = np.arange(max(int(gy[i] - r), 0), min(int(gy[i] + r) + 2, H))
        d2 = (xs[None, :] + 0.5 - gx[i]) ** 2 + (ys[:, None] + 0.5 - gy[i]) ** 2
        cap = np.sqrt(np.clip(r * r - d2, 0, None))
        zz = p[i, 2] + cap * s
        win = (slice(ys[0], ys[-1] + 1), slice(xs[0], xs[-1] + 1))
        upd = (d2 < r * r) & (zz > depth[win])
        depth[win][upd] = zz[upd]; index[win][upd] = i; nz[win][upd] = (cap / r)[upd]
    hit = index >= 0
    img = np.ones((H, W, 3))
    shade_ = col[index.clip(0)] * (0.72 + 0.28 * nz)[..., None]           # Spherical shading
    dmin, dmax = depth[hit].min(), depth[hit].max()
    f = (fog * (dmax - depth) / (dmax - dmin)).clip(0, fog)[..., None]   # Fade distant atoms toward white
    img[hit] = (shade_ * (1 - f) + f)[hit]
    g = np.where(hit, grp[index.clip(0)], -1); d = np.where(hit, depth, dmin - 100)
    edge = np.zeros((H, W), bool)
    for sh in ((0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1), (-1, 0)):                       # Outline component boundaries and depth steps
        g2, d3 = np.roll(g, sh, axis=(0, 1)), np.roll(d, sh, axis=(0, 1))
        edge |= hit & ((g2 != g) | (np.abs(d3 - d) > depth_jump)) & (d >= d3)
    for _ in range(line):
        edge |= np.roll(edge, 1, 0) | np.roll(edge, 1, 1)
    img[edge & hit] = 0.15
    img = img[:H // ss * ss, :W // ss * ss].reshape(H // ss, ss, W // ss, ss, 3).mean(axis=(1, 3))
    return img.clip(0, 1), [lo[0], hi[0], lo[1], hi[1]]

# (a) Side view, rotated 30° from the direction of subunit A
toA = xyz[chain_no == 0].mean(axis=0) - center; toA -= np.dot(toA, axis) * axis; toA /= np.linalg.norm(toA)
side_dir = np.cos(np.pi / 6) * toA + np.sin(np.pi / 6) * np.cross(axis, toA)
img_a, ext_a = render(np.ones(len(records), bool), view_matrix(side_dir, axis))
# (b) View from CII; remove material above S431/T432, retaining all CII-bound ATP
cut = height[kind == "phos"].max() + 1.0
img_b, ext_b = render((height <= cut) | (kind == "ATP_CII"), view_matrix(axis, toA), fog=0.45)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.5, 5.4), gridspec_kw=dict(width_ratios=[1.15, 1]))
ax[0].imshow(img_a, extent=ext_a); ax[1].imshow(img_b, extent=ext_b)
for a in ax:
    a.axis("off")
ax[0].set_title("(a) Side view of the hexamer", loc="left", fontsize=10.5)
ax[1].set_title("(b) CII section at S431/T432", loc="left", fontsize=10.5)
x_br = ext_a[1] + 2
for label, (y0, y1) in (("CII", (2, 50)), ("CI", (-50, -2))):
    ax[0].plot([x_br, x_br + 3, x_br + 3, x_br], [y0, y0, y1, y1], color=INK2, lw=1)
    ax[0].text(x_br + 5, (y0 + y1) / 2, label, va="center", fontsize=10.5)
ax[0].plot([ext_a[0] + 4, ext_a[0] + 54], [ext_a[2] - 3] * 2, color="#0b0b0b", lw=2)
ax[0].text(ext_a[0] + 29, ext_a[2] - 6, "5 nm", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=9)
ax[0].set(xlim=(ext_a[0] - 2, ext_a[1] + 16), ylim=(ext_a[2] - 13, ext_a[3] + 2))
fig.legend(handles=[Patch(color=rgb(PALETTE["CI"][0]), label="CI"), Patch(color=rgb(PALETTE["CII"][0]), label="CII"),
                    Patch(color=rgb(PALETTE["ATP"]), label="ATP"), Patch(color=rgb(PALETTE["phos"]), label="S431/T432")],
           loc="lower center", ncol=4, frameon=False, fontsize=9.5)
fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0.06, 1, 1))
plt.show()
```

Panel (b) of @fig-kaic shows the CII ring sliced at the height of S431 and T432 and viewed from above. The two phosphorylation sites, shown in magenta, face the subunit interfaces and lie next to ATP molecules, shown in yellow, bound to neighboring subunits. In this structure, the distance between ATP's terminal phosphorus atom and the side-chain oxygen of T432 is approximately `{python} f"{d_atp_t432.mean():.1f}"` Å. The phosphate group is thought to be transferred from ATP across the subunit interface [@egli2013].

KaiA and KaiB drive this directional cycle. KaiA binds to KaiC and stimulates its autophosphorylation. While KaiA is active, KaiC progresses from U to T and then ST. As S accumulates, however, KaiB binds to S-state KaiC, and the resulting complex sequesters KaiA, preventing it from acting [@rust2007]. Without KaiA, KaiC proceeds in the dephosphorylation direction, from ST through S to U. Eventually, the decline in S releases the sequestered KaiA, and phosphorylation begins again. Phosphorylation builds up S, which then shuts down phosphorylation itself. This delayed negative feedback generates the oscillation (@fig-cycle).

```{python}
#| label: fig-cycle
#| fig-cap: "The KaiC phosphorylation cycle and feedback through KaiA and KaiB. KaiA promotes phosphorylation along U → T → ST. S-state KaiC, together with KaiB, sequesters KaiA and stops phosphorylation."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Figure code"
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, FancyArrowPatch, FancyBboxPatch

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.set(xlim=(0, 11.6), ylim=(0, 7.2), aspect="equal")
ax.axis("off")

pos = {"U": (2.2, 1.4), "T": (2.2, 4.6), "ST": (6.2, 4.6), "S": (6.2, 1.4)}
r = 0.62
for name, (x, y) in pos.items():
    ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), r, facecolor="#f3f2ee", edgecolor=MUTED, lw=1.2, zorder=3))
    ax.text(x, y, name, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=14, zorder=4)

def arrow(p, q, color=INK2, style="-|>", ls="-", rad=0.0, lw=1.6, shrink=0.0):
    a = FancyArrowPatch(p, q, arrowstyle=style, mutation_scale=16, color=color, lw=lw,
                        linestyle=ls, connectionstyle=f"arc3,rad={rad}",
                        shrinkA=shrink, shrinkB=shrink, zorder=2)
    ax.add_patch(a)

def edge(a, b):  # arrow between two circles, trimmed at the rims
    (x1, y1), (x2, y2) = pos[a], pos[b]
    d = np.hypot(x2 - x1, y2 - y1); ux, uy = (x2 - x1) / d, (y2 - y1) / d
    arrow((x1 + ux * r, y1 + uy * r), (x2 - ux * r, y2 - uy * r))

for a, b in [("U", "T"), ("T", "ST"), ("ST", "S"), ("S", "U")]:
    edge(a, b)
lab = dict(fontsize=9, color=INK2, ha="center", va="center")
ax.text(1.9, 3.0, "T432\nphosphorylation", **{**lab, "ha": "right"})
ax.text(4.2, 3.85, "S431\nphosphorylation", **lab)
ax.text(6.5, 3.0, "T432\ndephosphorylation", **{**lab, "ha": "left"})
ax.text(4.2, 0.45, "S431\ndephosphorylation", **lab)

def box(x, y, text, fc, ec):
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((x - 0.65, y - 0.32), 1.3, 0.64, boxstyle="round,pad=0.05",
                                facecolor=fc, edgecolor=ec, lw=1.2, zorder=3))
    ax.text(x, y, text, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=12, zorder=4)

box(4.2, 6.5, "KaiA", "#dbe8f8", BLUE)
box(9.2, 1.4, "KaiB", "#fbe1d6", ORANGE)
arrow((3.7, 6.2), (2.35, 3.15), color=BLUE)             # KaiA -> U→T
arrow((4.2, 6.15), (4.2, 4.75), color=BLUE)             # KaiA -> T→ST
ax.text(2.9, 5.75, "Activation", fontsize=10, color=BLUE, ha="right")
arrow((6.85, 1.4), (8.5, 1.4), color=ORANGE, style="-", ls="--")    # S — KaiB
ax.text(7.7, 1.65, "Binding", fontsize=10, color=ORANGE, ha="center")
ax.plot([9.2, 9.2, 4.95], [1.75, 6.5, 6.5], color=ORANGE, lw=1.6, ls="--", zorder=1)  # S–KaiB inhibits KaiA
ax.plot([4.95, 4.95], [6.22, 6.78], color=ORANGE, lw=2.2, zorder=1)                       # Inhibition symbol
ax.text(9.35, 4.3, "Sequesters KaiA\nwith KaiB", fontsize=10, color=ORANGE, ha="left", va="center")
plt.show()
```

KaiC has another property essential to understanding temperature compensation. It is also an ATP-hydrolyzing enzyme, or ATPase, but an extraordinarily slow one. Each KaiC subunit hydrolyzes only about 15 ATP molecules per day, and this activity is itself temperature-compensated [@terauchi2007]. The left panel of @fig-atpase shows ATPase activity from 25 to 35 °C. Its Q~10~ is approximately 1.0 for KaiC alone and about 1.2 even with KaiA and KaiB present, clearly different from the dashed line representing a reaction with Q~10~ = 2. Furthermore, measurements across KaiC mutants with different periods showed that ATPase activity was proportional to the frequency of their in vivo rhythms, the reciprocal of the period (@fig-atpase, right). The faster the KaiC ATPase, the faster the clock.

```{python}
#| label: fig-atpase
#| fig-cap: "KaiC ATPase activity. Left: temperature dependence. Right: ATPase activity versus in vivo rhythm frequency for wild type and five period mutants; parentheses give their in vivo periods. Values were read from Figs. 4 and 5 of Terauchi et al. (2007) and replotted."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Figure code"
T = [25, 30, 35]
atp = {"KaiC alone": [15.35, 15.92, 14.75],
       "KaiC + KaiA + KaiB": [14.52, 16.67, 17.69],
       "KaiC-AA": [28.12, 27.14, 28.84],
       "KaiC-DE": [10.73, 10.71, 11.47]}
mutants = {"WT": (25, 1.00), "T42S": (28, 0.90), "S157P": (21, 1.37),
           "F470Y": (17, 1.55), "R393C": (15, 2.13), "A251V": (46, 0.30)}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2)
for (name, v), c in zip(atp.items(), [BLUE, ORANGE, AQUA, YELLOW]):
    ax[0].plot(T, v, "o-", color=c, ms=7, label=f"{name} (Q10 ≈ {v[2] / v[0]:.2f})")
ax[0].plot(T, 15.35 * np.array([1, 2 ** 0.5, 2]), "--", color=MUTED, lw=1, label="If Q10 = 2")
ax[0].set(xticks=T, ylim=(0, 46), xlabel="Temperature (°C)", ylabel="ATP hydrolysis (molecules / KaiC / day)")
ax[0].legend(fontsize=8.2, loc="upper center", ncol=2)

freq = np.array([24 / p for p, _ in mutants.values()])
act = np.array([a for _, a in mutants.values()])
slope = (freq @ act) / (freq @ freq)
x = np.linspace(0, 1.8, 10)
ax[1].plot(x, slope * x, color=MUTED, lw=1)
ax[1].plot(freq, act, "o", color="#0b0b0b", ms=7)
for (name, (p, a)), f in zip(mutants.items(), freq):
    ax[1].text(f + 0.03, a - 0.08, f"{name} ({p} h)", fontsize=8.5, color=INK2)
ax[1].set(xlim=(0, 2), ylim=(0, 2.5), xlabel="In vivo rhythm frequency (1/day)",
          ylabel="ATPase activity / wild-type activity")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Why is this activity so slow and so insensitive to temperature? A detailed structural study of the CI domain identified two causes of the slow rate: the water molecule used for hydrolysis is held in an unfavorable position for the reaction, and ATP hydrolysis is coupled to peptide-bond isomerization with a high activation energy [@abe2015]. The same study reported that ATPase activity shortly after adding ATP to KaiC alone, within the first two hours, was temperature-dependent (Q~10~ ≈ 1.4), whereas steady-state activity after at least 24 hours was almost temperature-independent (Q~10~ ≈ 1.1). A single amino-acid substitution in KaiC can also change the period over a range from 15 to 158 hours, while temperature compensation remains largely intact in many of these mutants [@itomiwa2020].

The connection between ATPase activity and period has also been tested with respect to temperature. In KaiC mutants whose ATPase activity lost temperature compensation, compensation of the phosphorylation rhythm's frequency broke down in the same direction [@furuike2022]. In three mutants with ATPase Q~10~ values elevated to 1.5–1.7, frequency Q~10~ values also rose, to 1.2–1.6. In a mutant whose ATPase instead slowed down as temperature increased (Q~10~ ≈ 0.5), frequency also decreased with temperature (Q~10~ ≈ 0.7). In addition, spontaneous dissociation of the KaiB–KaiC complex in the absence of KaiA is slow and temperature-compensated (Q~10~ ≈ 1.05) [@simon2022]. Several of the clock's components are intrinsically insensitive to temperature.

These observations might suggest that the secret of temperature compensation lies entirely in a single component, KaiC. But compensation of ATPase activity does not, by itself, explain why the period of the whole clock is compensated. Many reactions within and outside KaiC remain temperature-sensitive, and we need to understand how they determine the period when connected as a network. More fundamentally, what mathematical condition does "the period is independent of temperature" impose on a system with many reactions? The next section formulates that condition.

## Expressing temperature compensation mathematically {#sec-math}

### Temperature dependence of reactions

The temperature dependence of a chemical reaction's rate constant $k$ is often well described by the Arrhenius equation:

$$
k(T) = A \exp\left(-\frac{E}{RT}\right)
$$ {#eq-arrhenius}

Here, $T$ is absolute temperature, $R$ is the gas constant, $E$ is the activation energy, and $A$ is a constant with little temperature dependence. Think of the activation energy as the height of an energy barrier that the reaction must cross. The higher the barrier, the more strongly the reaction accelerates when temperature rises.

From @eq-arrhenius, the ratio of reaction rates when temperature rises from $T$ to $T + 10$ K, namely the reaction's Q~10~, is given by

$$
\ln Q_{10} = \frac{E}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T} - \frac{1}{T+10}\right) \approx \frac{10\,E}{RT^{2}}
$$ {#eq-q10}

For example, a reaction with an activation energy of 50 kJ/mol becomes approximately 1.9 times faster when warmed from 25 to 35 °C. @fig-q10 shows the relationship between activation energy and Q~10~. A period Q~10~ close to 1 means that the clock as a whole behaves like a reaction with an activation energy close to zero.

```{python}
#| label: fig-q10
#| fig-cap: "Activation energy versus Q~10~ from 25 to 35 °C. The yellow band marks the typical range of period Q~10~ for circadian rhythms."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.6
R = 8.314e-3                  # Gas constant (kJ / mol / K)
T1, T2 = 298.15, 308.15       # 25 and 35 °C
E = np.linspace(0, 120, 200)  # Activation energy (kJ/mol)
Q10 = np.exp(E / R * (1 / T1 - 1 / T2))

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.axhspan(0.8, 1.2, color=YELLOW, alpha=0.25, lw=0)
ax.plot(E, Q10, color=BLUE)
ax.plot(50, np.exp(50 / R * (1 / T1 - 1 / T2)), "o", color=ORANGE)
ax.annotate("E = 50 kJ/mol: Q10 ≈ 1.9", (50, 1.92), (58, 1.45), color=INK2,
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=MUTED))
ax.set(xlabel="Activation energy E (kJ/mol)", ylabel="Q10", ylim=(0.8, 5))
plt.show()
```

### Period control coefficients

The clock's period $\tau$ depends on the rate constants $k_1, k_2, \dots, k_n$ of many reactions in the network. We quantify the influence of each rate constant on the period by

$$
C_i = \frac{\partial \ln \tau}{\partial \ln k_i}
$$ {#eq-cc}

$C_i$ is the percentage change in period caused by a 1% change in the rate constant of reaction $i$, and is called a *period control coefficient*. It applies to the period an idea from metabolic control analysis, originally developed to measure how strongly individual enzymes control flux through a metabolic network [@ruoff2003]. If $C_i$ is negative, accelerating that reaction shortens the period, as we might ordinarily expect. If $C_i$ is positive, accelerating it instead lengthens the period.

Control coefficients have a simple but important property. Suppose we accelerate all reaction rate constants by the same factor $\lambda$. This is equivalent to watching the clock in fast-forward. Neither the order of reactions nor the shapes of the concentration trajectories change; only the time axis shrinks by a factor of $1/\lambda$. The period therefore also scales by $1/\lambda$:

$$
\tau(\lambda k_1, \dots, \lambda k_n) = \frac{\tau(k_1, \dots, k_n)}{\lambda}
$$

Taking logarithms of both sides, differentiating with respect to $\ln\lambda$, and setting $\lambda = 1$ gives

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} C_i = -1
$$ {#eq-sum}

This is called the *summation theorem*. Here, "all reactions" means all rate constants whose units contain inverse time. Parameters with concentration units, such as binding dissociation constants, and protein concentrations themselves do not change when we fast-forward the system, so they are excluded from this sum.

### The condition for temperature compensation

We now have everything we need. When temperature changes, each rate constant changes according to @eq-arrhenius, and its effect on the period is transmitted through its control coefficient. Applying the chain rule and substituting $d\ln k_i/dT = E_i/RT^2$ gives

$$
\frac{d \ln \tau}{d T} = \sum_{i} \frac{\partial \ln \tau}{\partial \ln k_i}\,\frac{d \ln k_i}{d T} = \frac{1}{RT^{2}} \sum_{i} C_i E_i
$$ {#eq-dlntau}

For the period to be independent of temperature, the sum on the right must vanish:

$$
\sum_{i} C_i E_i \approx 0
$$ {#eq-tc}

This is the condition for temperature compensation [@ruoff2003; @ruoff2005]. It can be understood as a ledger: enter each reaction's effect on the period as "control coefficient × activation energy," and balance the entries so that their total is zero.

What follows when we combine this ledger with the summation theorem, @eq-sum? If every reaction has the same activation energy $E$, then $\sum_i C_i E_i = E\sum_i C_i = -E$, and the period shortens with temperature just as it would for a single reaction with activation energy $E$. Network complexity alone cannot produce temperature compensation. Because activation energies are usually positive, canceling the contributions of reactions with negative control coefficients requires reactions with positive control coefficients: reactions that lengthen the period when accelerated. Their activation energies must also be sufficiently large. In a clock with many temperature-sensitive reactions, compensation thus arises from a thermal balance between reactions that shorten the period and reactions that lengthen it.

This conclusion has two assumptions. First, every reaction accelerates with temperature: its activation energy is positive. If we allow temperature-dependent equilibrium constants, discussed next, or processes with negative apparent activation energies, positive entries in the ledger can arise in other ways. Second, the activation energies are appreciably greater than zero. If all activation energies are nearly zero, the period is temperature-independent to begin with, even without period-lengthening reactions. The "uniformly insensitive" strategy in Section 7, and the view that KaiC ATPase activity is itself temperature-compensated, are closer to this possibility. The idea of balancing opposing effects has long been proposed as the *balance hypothesis* [@ruoff1992]. More recent work has investigated the conditions under which period-lengthening reactions arise in biochemical oscillators in general [@fu2024].

### Contributions from equilibrium constants

There is one more type of term to consider: processes such as molecular binding that are described by equilibrium constants rather than rate constants. The temperature dependence of an equilibrium constant $K$ follows the van 't Hoff equation,

$$
\frac{d \ln K}{d T} = \frac{\Delta H}{R T^{2}}
$$

where $\Delta H$ is the reaction enthalpy change. If $C_K$ is the period control coefficient for $K$, then @eq-dlntau acquires a term $C_K\,\Delta H$:

$$
\frac{d \ln \tau}{d T} = \frac{1}{RT^{2}}\left(\sum_i C_i E_i + \sum_j C_{K_j} \Delta H_j\right)
$$ {#eq-dlntau-full}

Unlike activation energies, $\Delta H$ can be either positive or negative. Temperature-induced shifts in binding equilibria can therefore provide another way to balance the ledger. In the model used here, the binding parameter governing KaiA's effect enters in this way.

@eq-tc tells us what temperature compensation requires. But looking at the equation alone cannot reveal which reactions shorten the period of the KaiABC clock and which lengthen it. To find out, we need to run a model of the clock.

## Running a KaiABC model {#sec-model}

We now turn to a mathematical model of the KaiABC clock and run it in Python. We use the model proposed by Rust and colleagues in 2007 [@rust2007]. They measured the rates of individual transitions between KaiC phosphorylation states, both with and without KaiA. Combining the resulting rate constants was sufficient to reproduce the in vitro oscillations fairly well. The model has only three variables, yet captures the essential behavior of the KaiABC clock. It does not, however, explicitly include the KaiC ATPase step. Its rate constants are effective parameters that combine multiple processes, including ATP hydrolysis. This distinction will matter when we consider the role of ATPase later.

### Model equations

The variables are the concentrations $T$, $D$, and $S$ of KaiC in the T, ST, and S states. We use $D$ for ST, from *doubly phosphorylated*. The U-state concentration follows by subtracting the other states from total KaiC: $U = [\mathrm{KaiC}] - T - D - S$. All transitions between the four states are written as first-order reactions:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dT}{dt} &= k_{UT}\,U + k_{DT}\,D - (k_{TU} + k_{TD})\,T \\
\frac{dD}{dt} &= k_{TD}\,T + k_{SD}\,S - (k_{DT} + k_{DS})\,D \\
\frac{dS}{dt} &= k_{US}\,U + k_{DS}\,D - (k_{SU} + k_{SD})\,S
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-rust}

$k_{XY}$ is the rate constant for the transition from state X to state Y. Besides the four arrows in @fig-cycle, the equations include reverse transitions, such as dephosphorylation from T to U.

Feedback enters because these rate constants depend on the amount of free KaiA. As we saw in Section 2, S-state KaiC sequesters KaiA together with KaiB. The original paper assumes that each S-state KaiC monomer sequesters one KaiA dimer, or two KaiA monomers, and writes the free KaiA concentration as

$$
A = \max\{0,\ [\mathrm{KaiA}] - 2S\}
$$ {#eq-freeA}

KaiB does not appear explicitly in the equations. It is assumed to be abundant and to bind rapidly to S-state KaiC, so its effect is incorporated into @eq-freeA. Each rate constant then depends hyperbolically on the amount of free KaiA:

$$
k_{XY} = k^{0}_{XY} + k^{A}_{XY}\,\frac{A}{K_{1/2} + A}
$$ {#eq-kxy}

$k^0_{XY}$ is the rate in the absence of KaiA, $k^A_{XY}$ is the change in rate at maximal KaiA stimulation, and $K_{1/2}$ is the KaiA concentration at which its effect is half-maximal.

In this article, we use a slightly rearranged version of @eq-kxy. Because $f = A/(K_{1/2} + A)$ can be interpreted as the fraction of KaiC bound to KaiA, we can write

$$
k_{XY} = (1 - f)\,k^{\mathrm{free}}_{XY} + f\,k^{\mathrm{bound}}_{XY},
\qquad k^{\mathrm{free}}_{XY} = k^{0}_{XY},\quad k^{\mathrm{bound}}_{XY} = k^{0}_{XY} + k^{A}_{XY}
$$ {#eq-kxy2}

This is a weighted average of the rates for KaiA-free and KaiA-bound KaiC, using their respective fractions. Written this way, each rate constant describes how fast KaiC in a particular state changes, making it easier to apply the Arrhenius equation in the next section.

@tbl-params lists the rate constants from the original paper's supplementary material, converted to this form. The calculated ST → S and S → U rates in the KaiA-bound state are slightly negative. Under the conditions used here, with 1.3 µM KaiA, the bound fraction never exceeds approximately 75%, so even the original model never gives a negative overall reaction rate. From the next section onward, however, we apply the Arrhenius equation to individual rate constants, which cannot be negative. We therefore set these two values to zero. This changes the period at 30 °C from approximately 20.7 to 21.4 hours.^[The original paper also sets an overall reaction rate to zero if it would otherwise become negative. That adjustment was needed only in some calculations at high KaiA concentrations.]

| Transition | Without KaiA $k^{\mathrm{free}}$ (h^−1^) | With KaiA $k^{\mathrm{bound}}$ (h^−1^) |
|:--|--:|--:|
| U → T | 0 | 0.479 |
| T → ST | 0 | 0.213 |
| S → ST | 0 | 0.506 |
| U → S | 0 | 0.053 |
| T → U | 0.21 | 0.290 |
| ST → T | 0 | 0.173 |
| ST → S | 0.31 | 0 (originally −0.009) |
| S → U | 0.11 | 0 (originally −0.023) |

: Rate constants in the Rust model, converted from Table S2 of the original supplementary material to the form in @eq-kxy2. $K_{1/2}$ = 0.43 µM, KaiA = 1.3 µM, and KaiC = 3.4 µM. {#tbl-params}

The table reveals the character of the model. Transitions in the phosphorylation direction—U → T, T → ST, S → ST, and U → S—occur only when KaiA is bound. Conversely, dephosphorylation through ST → S and S → U occurs only when KaiA is not bound. Whether KaiA is free to act switches the entire system between phosphorylation and dephosphorylation phases.

We now implement this in code. The functions accept arrays of parameters so that many parameter sets can be simulated at once.

```{python}
#| label: model
R_GAS = 8.314e-3                     # Gas constant (kJ / mol / K)
KAIA, KAIC, KHALF = 1.3, 3.4, 0.43   # Concentrations (µM)

# Nine nonzero rate constants (1/h): _b for KaiA-bound, _f for KaiA-free
RATES0 = {"UT_b": 0.479077, "TD_b": 0.212923, "SD_b": 0.505692, "US_b": 0.0532308,
          "TU_b": 0.21 + 0.0798462, "DT_b": 0.173,
          "TU_f": 0.21, "DS_f": 0.31, "SU_f": 0.11}
RATE_NAMES = list(RATES0)
LABELS = {"UT_b": "U→T (KaiA)", "TD_b": "T→ST (KaiA)", "SD_b": "S→ST (KaiA)",
          "US_b": "U→S (KaiA)", "TU_b": "T→U (KaiA)", "DT_b": "ST→T (KaiA)",
          "TU_f": "T→U (no KaiA)", "DS_f": "ST→S (no KaiA)", "SU_f": "S→U (no KaiA)"}

def base_params():
    return {**RATES0, "KHALF": KHALF, "KAIA": KAIA, "KAIC": KAIC}

def rhs(x, P):
    """Right-hand side of eq-rust. Array x has shape (3, N) for N parameter sets."""
    T, D, S = x
    U = P["KAIC"] - T - D - S
    A = np.maximum(0.0, P["KAIA"] - 2.0 * S)          # Free KaiA
    f = A / (P["KHALF"] + A)                          # Fraction bound to KaiA
    g = 1.0 - f
    kUT, kTD, kSD, kUS = f * P["UT_b"], f * P["TD_b"], f * P["SD_b"], f * P["US_b"]
    kTU = f * P["TU_b"] + g * P["TU_f"]
    kDT = f * P["DT_b"]
    kDS, kSU = g * P["DS_f"], g * P["SU_f"]
    dT = kUT * U + kDT * D - (kTU + kTD) * T
    dD = kTD * T + kSD * S - (kDT + kDS) * D
    dS = kUS * U + kDS * D - (kSU + kSD) * S
    return np.array([dT, dD, dS])
```

We solve the differential equations using the fourth-order Runge–Kutta method. As in the original paper, the initial concentrations are 0.68 µM T, 1.36 µM ST, and 0.34 µM S. After allowing enough time for the oscillations to settle, we measure the period from upward crossings of the mean total phosphorylated KaiC concentration, $T + D + S$. Crossing times are found by linear interpolation, and the period is the mean interval between successive crossings.

```{python}
#| label: integrator
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Numerical integration and period measurement"
X0 = np.array([0.68, 1.36, 0.34])

def stack(params_list):
    """Convert a list of parameter dictionaries to a dictionary of arrays."""
    return {k: np.array([p[k] for p in params_list], float) for k in params_list[0]}

def integrate(P, t_end, dt=0.01, x0=None, record_every=10, forcing=None):
    """Integrate N parameter sets with RK4; forcing(t) returns parameters at time t."""
    N = np.size(P["KAIC"])
    x = np.tile(X0.reshape(3, 1), (1, N)) if x0 is None else np.array(x0, float).reshape(3, -1)
    ts, ys = [], []
    for i in range(int(round(t_end / dt))):
        t = i * dt
        if i % record_every == 0:
            ts.append(t); ys.append(x.copy())
        P1, P2, P3 = (forcing(t), forcing(t + dt / 2), forcing(t + dt)) if forcing else (P, P, P)
        k1 = rhs(x, P1); k2 = rhs(x + 0.5 * dt * k1, P2)
        k3 = rhs(x + 0.5 * dt * k2, P2); k4 = rhs(x + dt * k3, P3)
        x = x + dt / 6.0 * (k1 + 2 * k2 + 2 * k3 + k4)
    return np.array(ts), np.array(ys)          # ys has shape (time, 3, N)

def crossing_times(t, P):
    """Upward crossings of the mean of P, found by linear interpolation."""
    c = P - P.mean()
    i = np.where((c[:-1] < 0) & (c[1:] >= 0))[0]
    return t[i] - c[i] * (t[i + 1] - t[i]) / (c[i + 1] - c[i])

def period_amp_from(t, y, t_skip):
    """Period and amplitude (peak-to-trough T+D+S) for each parameter set; NaN and 0 if nonoscillatory."""
    m = t >= t_skip
    Ptot = y[m].sum(axis=1)
    half = len(Ptot) // 2
    per = np.full(Ptot.shape[1], np.nan)
    amp = np.zeros(Ptot.shape[1])
    for j in range(Ptot.shape[1]):
        a1, a2 = np.ptp(Ptot[:half, j]), np.ptp(Ptot[half:, j])
        if a2 < 1e-3 or a2 < 0.95 * a1:                   # No oscillation, or still decaying
            continue
        d = np.diff(crossing_times(t[m], Ptot[:, j]))
        if len(d) >= 2 and d.std() / d.mean() < 0.02:   # Count only regular oscillations
            per[j] = d.mean()
            amp[j] = np.ptp(Ptot[:, j])
    return per, amp

def period_amp(params_list, t_end=900.0, t_skip=500.0, dt=0.01):
    t, y = integrate(stack(params_list), t_end, dt)
    return period_amp_from(t, y, t_skip)
```

```{python}
#| label: run-30C
p0 = base_params()
tau0 = period_amp([p0])[0][0]
t, y = integrate(stack([p0]), 300, dt=0.01, record_every=5)
```

With the rate constants at 30 °C, the calculated period is `{python} f"{tau0:.1f}"` hours, in good agreement with the approximately 21-hour period measured by Nakajima and colleagues at that temperature [@nakajima2005]. @fig-timeseries shows the phosphorylation-state trajectories and the amount of free KaiA. The peaks occur in the order T, ST, and S, reproducing the U → T → ST → S → U sequence described in Section 2. Notice the free KaiA concentration: as S builds up, free KaiA abruptly reaches zero and remains there for a while. This is the dephosphorylation phase. Once S decreases and KaiA is released, the phosphorylation phase begins again.

```{python}
#| label: fig-timeseries
#| fig-cap: "Time courses of KaiC phosphorylation states at 30 °C (top) and free KaiA concentration (bottom). Three cycles are shown after the oscillations have settled."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Figure code"
m = (t >= 200) & (t <= 272)
tt, Y = t[m] - 200, y[m][:, :, 0]
T_, D_, S_ = Y.T
U_ = KAIC - T_ - D_ - S_
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 1, sharex=True, gridspec_kw=dict(height_ratios=[2.2, 1]))
for arr, lab, c in [(U_, "U", MUTED), (T_, "T", BLUE), (D_, "ST", ORANGE), (S_, "S", AQUA)]:
    ax[0].plot(tt, arr / KAIC, color=c, label=lab)
ax[0].set_ylabel("Fraction of total KaiC")
ax[0].legend(ncol=4, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 1.15))
ax[1].plot(tt, np.maximum(0, KAIA - 2 * S_), color=INK2)
ax[1].set(xlabel="Time (h)", ylabel="Free KaiA (µM)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The oscillation settles into the same shape regardless of its starting point. @fig-phase plots trajectories from two widely separated initial conditions, using S concentration and total phosphorylated KaiC as the axes. Both trajectories eventually move around the same closed loop. Such an isolated periodic orbit that attracts nearby trajectories is called a *limit cycle*. The description of a circadian clock as a limit cycle will underpin our discussion in Section 8 of how oscillations stop and how the clock entrains to temperature cycles.

```{python}
#| label: fig-phase
#| fig-cap: "Trajectories starting from two initial conditions (circles). Both approach the same limit cycle. The dashed line marks complete KaiA sequestration by S-state KaiC, S = [KaiA]/2."
#| fig-width: 5.4
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Figure code"
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for x0, c in [((0.05, 0.05, 0.05), BLUE), ((0.3, 2.2, 0.8), ORANGE)]:
    t2, y2 = integrate(stack([p0]), 250, dt=0.01, x0=np.array(x0), record_every=5)
    yy = y2[:, :, 0]
    ax.plot(yy[:, 2], yy.sum(axis=1), color=c, lw=1.2)
    ax.plot(yy[0, 2], yy[0].sum(), "o", color=c, ms=7)
ax.axvline(KAIA / 2, color=MUTED, ls="--", lw=1)
ax.set(xlabel="S-state KaiC (µM)", ylabel="Total phosphorylated KaiC, T+ST+S (µM)")
plt.show()
```

The dashed line in @fig-phase marks the boundary at which S sequesters all available KaiA. The limit cycle crosses this boundary, switching into the dephosphorylation phase as it does so. The original supplementary material also shows that oscillations require a sufficiently small $K_{1/2}$, in the range 0.092–0.93 µM, so that changes in KaiA concentration produce a sharp, switch-like change in reaction rates [@rust2007]. Sequestration itself creates strong nonlinearity, even without assuming cooperative binding.

We now have a working clock at 30 °C. Next, we change its temperature.

## Introducing temperature {#sec-naive}

To introduce temperature into the model, we give each of the nine rate constants in @tbl-params an Arrhenius temperature dependence using @eq-arrhenius. Taking the reference temperature $T_0$ to be 30 °C and requiring the rate constants to equal the tabulated values there gives

$$
k_i(T) = k_i(T_0)\,\exp\left[-\frac{E_i}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T} - \frac{1}{T_0}\right)\right]
$$ {#eq-arrhenius-ref}

Because $K_{1/2}$ is an equilibrium constant, we use the van 't Hoff equation when assigning its temperature dependence. Expressed relative to the reference temperature, it has the same mathematical form.

```{python}
#| label: at-temperature
T_REF = 30.0   # Reference temperature (°C)

def at_temperature(p, temp_c, E, H=0.0):
    """Parameters at temp_c (°C). E maps rate constants to activation energies (kJ/mol);
    H is the enthalpy change for K_1/2 (kJ/mol)."""
    T, T0 = temp_c + 273.15, T_REF + 273.15
    factor = lambda e: np.exp(-(e / R_GAS) * (1.0 / T - 1.0 / T0))
    q = dict(p)
    for n in RATE_NAMES:
        q[n] = p[n] * factor(E[n])
    q["KHALF"] = p["KHALF"] * factor(H)
    return q
```

As a first, naive attempt, we assign an activation energy of 50 kJ/mol to all nine reactions.

```{python}
#| label: naive-sweep
E_equal = {n: 50.0 for n in RATE_NAMES}
temps = np.arange(15.0, 40.01, 2.5)
per_eq, amp_eq = period_amp([at_temperature(p0, T, E_equal) for T in temps], t_end=1500, t_skip=900)
tau_at = lambda T: per_eq[np.argmin(abs(temps - T))]
q10_naive = tau_at(25) / tau_at(35)
q10_arrhenius = np.exp(50 / R_GAS * (1 / 298.15 - 1 / 308.15))
```

@fig-naive shows the result. The period decreases monotonically with temperature, giving a Q~10~ of `{python} f"{q10_naive:.3f}"` between 25 and 35 °C. This agrees exactly with the Q~10~ of a single reaction with an activation energy of 50 kJ/mol, `{python} f"{q10_arrhenius:.3f}"`, as predicted by the summation theorem in Section 3. Scaling every rate constant by the same factor simply fast-forwards the clock, so the period must decrease by that factor. In an Arrhenius plot of the logarithm of reciprocal period against reciprocal absolute temperature, shown on the right, the slope directly recovers the 50 kJ/mol activation energy. The squares on the left are the in vitro periods measured by Nakajima and colleagues [@nakajima2005]. The real clock's period shortens only slightly as temperature rises.

```{python}
#| label: fig-naive
#| fig-cap: "Period when every reaction has an activation energy of 50 kJ/mol. Left: period versus temperature; squares are measurements from Nakajima et al. (2005). Right: Arrhenius plot of reciprocal period."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Figure code"
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2)
ax[0].plot(temps, per_eq, "o-", color=ORANGE, ms=5, label="Model (all 50 kJ/mol)")
ax[0].plot([25, 30, 35], [22, 21, 20], "s", color="#0b0b0b", ms=7, label="In vitro measurements")
ax[0].set(xlabel="Temperature (°C)", ylabel="Period (h)")
ax[0].legend()
x = 1000 / (temps + 273.15)
yv = np.log(1 / per_eq)
slope, icpt = np.polyfit(x, yv, 1)
ax[1].plot(x, yv, "o", color=ORANGE, ms=5)
ax[1].plot(x, slope * x + icpt, color=INK2, lw=1)
ax[1].set(xlabel="1000 / T (1/K)", ylabel="ln(1 / period)")
ax[1].text(0.05, 0.08, f"E from slope = {-slope * R_GAS * 1000:.1f} kJ/mol",
           transform=ax[1].transAxes, color=INK2)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

As a clock, this model fails the test. Yet the failure teaches us something useful. Temperature compensation, if it occurs, must rely on differences between the reactions' activation energies, arranged so as to balance the ledger in @eq-tc. Where is there room to balance it? To answer that, we need to examine each reaction's control coefficient.

## Dissecting compensation through sensitivity analysis {#sec-sensitivity}

### Calculating control coefficients numerically

The control coefficients in @eq-cc are easy to calculate numerically. We increase and decrease each rate constant slightly, here by ±1% on a logarithmic scale, measure the period, and estimate the derivative from the difference using a central finite difference.

```{python}
#| label: control-coeffs
def control_coeffs(p, names, h=0.01):
    """Estimate C = d ln(period) / d ln(parameter) by central differences."""
    plist = []
    for n in names:
        for s in (+1, -1):
            q = dict(p)
            q[n] = p[n] * np.exp(s * h)
            plist.append(q)
    per, _ = period_amp(plist)
    return {n: (np.log(per[2 * i]) - np.log(per[2 * i + 1])) / (2 * h) for i, n in enumerate(names)}

C_all = control_coeffs(p0, RATE_NAMES + ["KHALF", "KAIA", "KAIC"])
C = {n: C_all[n] for n in RATE_NAMES}
Cv = np.array([C[n] for n in RATE_NAMES])
C_sum = Cv.sum()
```

@fig-cc shows the results. First, the control coefficients of the nine rate constants sum to `{python} f"{C_sum:.3f}"`, confirming the summation theorem in @eq-sum numerically. The control coefficients for the equilibrium constant $K_{1/2}$ and the KaiA and KaiC concentrations are `{python} f"{C_all['KHALF']:+.2f}"`, `{python} f"{C_all['KAIA']:+.2f}"`, and `{python} f"{C_all['KAIC']:+.2f}"`, respectively. These parameters are not rate constants, so their coefficients are excluded from the sum.

```{python}
#| label: fig-cc
#| fig-cap: "Control coefficients at 30 °C. Positive coefficients (orange) identify reactions that lengthen the period when accelerated; negative coefficients (blue) identify reactions that shorten it."
#| fig-width: 6.6
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Figure code"
order = np.argsort(Cv)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.barh([LABELS[RATE_NAMES[i]] for i in order], Cv[order],
        color=[ORANGE if c > 0 else BLUE for c in Cv[order]], height=0.62)
ax.axvline(0, color=INK2, lw=0.8)
for j, i in enumerate(order):
    ax.text(Cv[i] + (0.04 if Cv[i] >= 0 else -0.04), j, f"{Cv[i]:+.2f}", va="center",
            ha="left" if Cv[i] >= 0 else "right", fontsize=9, color=INK2)
ax.set(xlabel="Control coefficient C", xlim=(-1.6, 1.4))
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
plt.show()
```

Most reactions have negative control coefficients, as intuition suggests. Dephosphorylation from ST to S without KaiA shortens the period most strongly, with a coefficient of `{python} f"{C['DS_f']:+.2f}"`. Two reactions, however, have clearly positive coefficients: KaiA-dependent phosphorylation from S to ST, `{python} f"{C['SD_b']:+.2f}"`, and dephosphorylation from ST to T, `{python} f"{C['DT_b']:+.2f}"`. The two T → U reactions are also positive, but only weakly, at no more than `{python} f"{max(C['TU_b'], C['TU_f']):+.2f}"`. In particular, accelerating S → ST lengthens the period by nearly the same proportion. In Section 3, we argued that compensation requires reactions that lengthen the period when accelerated. In this model, S → ST can play that role.

### Why does S → ST lengthen the period?

The S → ST reaction pushes S-state KaiC back into the ST state. As discussed in Section 2, S cooperates with KaiB to sequester KaiA and stop phosphorylation. If S → ST is fast, S accumulates more slowly, delaying KaiA sequestration. Phosphorylation continues during this delay, producing more phosphorylated KaiC. Removing those additional phosphates during the subsequent dephosphorylation phase then takes longer as well. Both phases therefore lengthen.

```{python}
#| label: sd-mechanism
phase_rows = []
for factor in (0.8, 1.0, 1.25):
    q = dict(p0)
    q["SD_b"] = p0["SD_b"] * factor
    ts_, ys_ = integrate(stack([q]), 900, dt=0.01, record_every=1)
    keep = ts_ >= 500
    S_ = ys_[keep][:, 2, 0]
    per_ = period_amp_from(ts_, ys_, 500)[0][0]
    frac_free = np.mean(KAIA - 2 * S_ > 0)            # Fraction of time with free KaiA
    phase_rows.append((factor, per_, frac_free * per_, (1 - frac_free) * per_))
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-sd
#| fig-cap: "Time spent with free KaiA (phosphorylation phase) and sequestered KaiA (dephosphorylation phase) during one cycle as the S → ST rate changes."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 2.6
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Figure code"
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for k, (fac, per_, free_, capt_) in enumerate(phase_rows):
    ax.barh(k, free_, color=BLUE, height=0.55, label="KaiA free" if k == 0 else None)
    ax.barh(k, capt_, left=free_, color=ORANGE, height=0.55, label="KaiA sequestered" if k == 0 else None)
    ax.text(per_ + 0.3, k, f"Period {per_:.1f} h", va="center", fontsize=9, color=INK2)
ax.set_yticks(range(len(phase_rows)), [f"S→ST × {fac}" for fac, *_ in phase_rows])
ax.set(xlabel="Time (h)", xlim=(0, 33))
ax.legend(loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 1.16), ncol=2, fontsize=9)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
plt.show()
```

@fig-sd illustrates this. Increasing the S → ST rate by a factor of 1.25 extends the time with free KaiA from `{python} f"{phase_rows[1][2]:.1f}"` to `{python} f"{phase_rows[2][2]:.1f}"` hours, and the time with sequestered KaiA from `{python} f"{phase_rows[1][3]:.1f}"` to `{python} f"{phase_rows[2][3]:.1f}"` hours. The seemingly paradoxical slowing of the clock when a reaction is accelerated arises because the oscillation makes a larger excursion. Studying several oscillator models, Fu and colleagues showed that period-lengthening reactions generally emerge in strongly nonlinear regimes sufficiently far from the onset of oscillation, and that they lengthen the period by increasing the size of the oscillatory excursion [@fu2024]. Our result confirms the same mechanism in a different KaiABC model.

### Randomly sampling activation energies

Now that we know the control coefficients, we can ask how difficult it is to balance the ledger in @eq-tc. We generate 2,000 sets of activation energies for the nine reactions, randomly sampling each energy from 20 to 100 kJ/mol. For each set, we calculate Q~10~ from the periods at 25 and 35 °C.

```{python}
#| label: random-sampling
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
Es = rng.uniform(20, 100, size=(2000, len(RATE_NAMES)))
per25, _ = period_amp([at_temperature(p0, 25.0, dict(zip(RATE_NAMES, e))) for e in Es], t_end=1000, t_skip=600)
per35, _ = period_amp([at_temperature(p0, 35.0, dict(zip(RATE_NAMES, e))) for e in Es], t_end=1000, t_skip=600)
Q10s = per25 / per35
Q10_pred = np.exp(-(Es @ Cv) / R_GAS * (1 / 298.15 - 1 / 308.15))   # Prediction from the ledger
osc = np.isfinite(Q10s)
comp = osc & (Q10s > 0.9) & (Q10s < 1.1)
frac_comp = comp.sum() / osc.sum()
r_pred = np.corrcoef(np.log(Q10s[osc]), np.log(Q10_pred[osc]))[0, 1]
```

The results appear in @fig-random. Of the `{python} f"{osc.sum()}"` sets that oscillated at both temperatures, only `{python} f"{frac_comp * 100:.1f}"`% had Q~10~ values between 0.9 and 1.1. The median Q~10~ was `{python} f"{np.median(Q10s[osc]):.2f}"`: most sets sped up with temperature much like ordinary chemical reactions. The right panel compares simulated Q~10~ values with predictions from the control coefficients at 30 °C and @eq-dlntau. The correlation between their logarithms is `{python} f"{r_pred:.3f}"`. The ledger equation from Section 3 predicts the temperature dependence of this nonlinear model remarkably well.

```{python}

#| fig-cap: "Results for 2,000 randomly sampled activation-energy sets. Left: distribution of period Q~10~, with 0.9–1.1 shaded yellow. Right: ledger predictions versus simulations."

ax[0].hist(Q10s[osc], bins=bins, color=BLUE, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.6)
ax[0].axvspan(0.9, 1.1, color=YELLOW, alpha=0.3, lw=0)
ax[0].set(xscale="log", xlabel="Period Q10 (25 °C → 35 °C)", ylabel="Number of sets")
ax[1].loglog(Q10_pred[osc], Q10s[osc], ".", color=BLUE, ms=3, alpha=0.5)
ax[1].plot([0.2, 15], [0.2, 15], color=INK2, lw=1)
ax[1].set(xlim=(0.2, 15), ylim=(0.2, 15), xlabel="Q10 predicted by the ledger", ylabel="Simulated Q10")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

What distinguishes the compensated sets? @fig-features compares the mean activation energy of each reaction across all sets and across the compensated subset. Compensated sets have a higher activation energy for the period-lengthening S → ST reaction and a lower activation energy for ST → S without KaiA, the reaction that most strongly shortens the period. In ledger terms, they both enlarge a positive entry and reduce the largest negative entry.

```{python}

for j, i in enumerate(oo):
    ax.plot([Es[osc, i].mean(), Es[comp, i].mean()], [j, j], color=GRID, lw=3, zorder=1)
ax.plot(Es[osc][:, oo].mean(axis=0), yy, "o", color=MUTED, ms=8, label="All sets", zorder=2)

        label=f"Compensated sets (n = {comp.sum()})", zorder=3)
```

Temperature compensation is rare when activation energies are chosen at random. Building a compensated clock requires specific relationships among those energies. How might these relationships be arranged? And do they produce a clock that works across a broad temperature range and withstands mutations?

## Ways to balance the period ledger {#sec-strategies}

There is more than one way to balance @eq-tc. We begin with two strategies that are opposite in character. Both are extreme constructions that express an idea in its simplest possible form, so many of their differences follow directly from how they are built. Starting with these extremes nevertheless makes it easier to see how strongly the balancing strategy changes the clock's behavior. We consider intermediate strategies in Section 9.

The first strategy makes every activation energy small. Each term $C_i E_i$ is then small to begin with, so the ledger cannot become strongly unbalanced. As discussed in Section 2, KaiC ATPase activity and dissociation of the KaiB–KaiC complex are themselves temperature-compensated [@terauchi2007; @simon2022]. The idea is that if every component of the clock is insensitive to temperature, the whole clock will be too. Here, we call a clock with all activation energies except that of S → ST set to 10 kJ/mol, corresponding to a reaction-rate Q~10~ of about 1.1, the *uniformly insensitive strategy*. This is the simplest realization of that idea, however, and is not identical to the hypothesis that ATPase determines the period. That hypothesis requires compensation of the reactions controlling the period, without requiring every reaction to be temperature-insensitive. This distinction becomes important in Section 9.

The second strategy gives the reactions typical activation energies of 50 kJ/mol, corresponding to Q~10~ ≈ 1.9, and makes the activation energy of the period-lengthening S → ST reaction especially large so that positive and negative entries cancel. The idea that temperature compensation results from balancing reactions with opposing thermal effects dates back to Hastings and Sweeney [@hastings1957]; Ruoff subsequently extended it to general reaction models [@ruoff1992]. We call this direct realization of the balance hypothesis the *cancellation strategy*.

In both strategies, we choose the activation energy of S → ST so that the ledger $\sum_i C_i E_i$ is exactly zero at 30 °C.

```{python}
#| label: strategies
def balance_E(E_base, E_sensor=None):
    """Set activation energies other than S→ST to E_base; override U→T if E_sensor is given.
    Choose S→ST to balance the period ledger at 30 °C."""
    E = {n: E_base for n in RATE_NAMES}
    if E_sensor is not None:
        E["UT_b"] = E_sensor
    E["SD_b"] = -sum(C[n] * E[n] for n in RATE_NAMES if n != "SD_b") / C["SD_b"]
    return E

STRATEGIES = {"A": balance_E(10.0), "B": balance_E(50.0)}
NAMES = {"A": "A: Insensitive", "B": "B: Cancellation", "C": "C: Coupled", "R": "R: Division of labor"}
COLORS = {"A": BLUE, "B": ORANGE, "C": "#a3401a", "R": AQUA}

def q10_rate(E):
    """Rate Q10 from 25 to 35 °C for a reaction with activation energy E (kJ/mol)."""
    return np.exp(E / R_GAS * (1 / 298.15 - 1 / 308.15))
```

@fig-ledger compares the two ledgers. The S → ST activation energy is `{python} f"{STRATEGIES['A']['SD_b']:.0f}"` kJ/mol in the uniformly insensitive strategy and `{python} f"{STRATEGIES['B']['SD_b']:.0f}"` kJ/mol in the cancellation strategy. Both sums are zero, but one consists of small entries, while the other cancels large entries against one another.

```{python}

for ax, key in zip(axes, ("A", "B")):

    ax.barh([LABELS[n] for n in RATE_NAMES], contrib,
            color=[ORANGE if c > 0 else BLUE for c in contrib], height=0.62)
    ax.axvline(0, color=INK2, lw=0.8)
    ax.set_axisbelow(True)

    ax.set_xlabel("Contribution (kJ/mol)")
    ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### Temperature range

We vary temperature from 0 to 50 °C in both strategies (@fig-strategies-temp).

```{python}
sweep = {}
for key in ("A", "B"):
    per, amp = period_amp([at_temperature(p0, T, STRATEGIES[key]) for T in temps_wide], t_end=2000, t_skip=1300)
    ok = np.isfinite(per)
    sweep[key] = dict(per=per, amp=amp, lo=temps_wide[ok].min(), hi=temps_wide[ok].max())
amp_ratio_A = sweep["A"]["amp"][np.argmin(abs(temps_wide - 20))] / sweep["A"]["amp"][np.argmin(abs(temps_wide - 30))]
```

The uniformly insensitive strategy continues to oscillate with almost the same period from `{python} f"{sweep['A']['lo']:.1f}"` °C to `{python} f"{sweep['A']['hi']:.0f}"` °C, the upper limit tested. This is unsurprising, since every reaction is relatively temperature-insensitive. The cancellation strategy, in contrast, oscillates only from `{python} f"{sweep['B']['lo']:.1f}"` to `{python} f"{sweep['B']['hi']:.1f}"` °C. Its ledger was balanced only at 30 °C. Away from that temperature, the ratios between reaction rates change substantially, eventually making oscillation impossible. The amplitudes also behave differently. The uniformly insensitive strategy's amplitude changes only gradually with temperature and still retains `{python} f"{amp_ratio_A * 100:.0f}"`% of its 30 °C value at 20 °C. The cancellation strategy's amplitude falls rapidly as temperature decreases. This distinction will matter in the next section.

### Robustness to mutations

We also compare robustness to mutations. In real KaiC, a single amino-acid substitution can greatly change the period while leaving temperature compensation largely intact [@itomiwa2020]. We therefore construct "mutants" by multiplying each of ten parameters—the nine rate constants and $K_{1/2}$—by either 0.67 or 1.5, one at a time, and examine their Q~10~ values while leaving activation energies unchanged. We convert the periods at 28 and 32 °C to Q~10~, and also count mutants that lose oscillation at either 25 or 35 °C.

```{python}
#| label: mutation
def mutation_test(p, E, temps=(25.0, 28.0, 32.0, 35.0)):
    """Test Q10 and loss of oscillations in 20 mutants, scaling one parameter at a time by 0.67 or 1.5."""
    plist = []
    for n in RATE_NAMES + ["KHALF"]:
        for fac in (0.67, 1.5):
            q = dict(p)
            q[n] = p[n] * fac
            plist += [at_temperature(q, T, E) for T in temps]
    per, _ = period_amp(plist, t_end=2000, t_skip=1300)
    per = per.reshape(-1, len(temps))
    q10_local = (per[:, 1] / per[:, 2]) ** 2.5                 # Convert the periods at 28 °C and 32 °C to Q10
    lost = np.isnan(per[:, 0]) | np.isnan(per[:, 3])
    return dict(q10=q10_local, lost=int(lost.sum()), n=len(per),
                med=np.nanmedian(np.abs(np.log(q10_local))))

mut = {key: mutation_test(p0, STRATEGIES[key]) for key in ("A", "B")}
```

```{python}
jitter = np.random.default_rng(0)
for k, key in enumerate(("A", "B")):
    q = mut[key]["q10"]
    fin = np.isfinite(q)
    ax.scatter(k + jitter.uniform(-0.15, 0.15, fin.sum()), q[fin], s=28, color=COLORS[key],
               edgecolor="white", lw=0.8, zorder=3)
    ax.text(k, 1.33, f"Stopped: {mut[key]['lost']}/{mut[key]['n']}", ha="center", fontsize=9, color=INK2)
ax.axhspan(0.9, 1.1, color=YELLOW, alpha=0.25, lw=0)
ax.set_xticks(range(2), [NAMES[k] for k in ("A", "B")])
ax.set(xlim=(-0.6, 1.6), ylim=(0.3, 1.42), ylabel="Mutant Q10")
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
```
