
@fig-mutation shows the results. Under the uniformly insensitive strategy, Q~10~ stays near 1 in most mutants, with a median $|\ln Q_{10}|$ of `{python} f"{mut['A']['med']:.3f}"`, and `{python} f"{mut['A']['lost']}"` mutants lose oscillation at 25 or 35 °C. Under the cancellation strategy, Q~10~ varies much more widely, with a median $|\ln Q_{10}|$ of `{python} f"{mut['B']['med']:.3f}"`. A ledger balanced by canceling large entries can become unbalanced after a small mutation-induced change in the control coefficients. In addition, `{python} f"{mut['B']['lost']}"` mutants lose oscillation. The unmutated cancellation strategy already fails to oscillate below 24.5 °C, however, so 25 °C lies at the edge of its operating range. This count reflects both sensitivity to mutation and the narrow range of oscillation before mutation.

These results apply specifically to this strategy, which balances large entries at a single temperature, 30 °C. As we will see in Section 8, this operating point is not far from the bifurcation at approximately 24 °C where oscillation stops. Fu and colleagues report that compensation through period-lengthening reactions can hold across a broad range of parameters sufficiently far from the onset of oscillation [@fu2024]. The fragility observed here must therefore reflect not only cancellation itself but also this model's proximity to a bifurcation. Compensation by cancellation is not necessarily fragile in every case. Also, our simulated mutations change only the magnitudes of rate constants, leaving activation energies unchanged. In real proteins, a single mutation can change the temperature dependence of a reaction itself [@furuike2022].

A broad temperature range and robustness to mutations: so far, the uniformly insensitive strategy seems to make the better clock. But as noted in Section 1, a clock has another important property besides resisting the effects of temperature. It must also sense temperature.

## A clock must sense temperature {#sec-sensing}

Two experimental observations show that the clock senses temperature: it stops when cooled, and it entrains to temperature cycles.

### The clock stops at low temperature

Temperature compensation does not mean that the clock works at every temperature. Murayama and colleagues gradually cooled the in vitro KaiABC clock and examined its behavior in detail [@murayama2017]. As temperature fell, the amplitude decreased markedly while the period changed little, until oscillations disappeared at approximately 19 °C. Below that temperature, an external perturbation elicited oscillations that decayed with time: damped oscillations. Single-cell observations have shown that clocks in living cells also stop at low temperature through the same type of bifurcation [@mihalcescu2025]. Theory anticipated this behavior before the experiments. In the model of Hatakeyama and Kaneko, temperature compensation arises because multiple reactions compete for a limited amount of KaiA; cooling reduces the amplitude and eventually eliminates oscillation through a Hopf bifurcation [@hatakeyama2012].

There are two typical ways for an oscillation to disappear. In one, the amplitude gradually goes to zero while the period remains finite: a *Hopf bifurcation*. In the other, the amplitude is retained while the period grows without bound: a *SNIC bifurcation*, or saddle-node bifurcation on an invariant circle. The experimental disappearance of amplitude at an almost constant period points to a Hopf bifurcation.

For later comparison with the model, we extract periods and amplitudes at each temperature from the figure in Murayama and colleagues' paper.

```{python}
#| label: murayama-data
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Experimental data (values read from Fig. 2B of Murayama et al. 2017)"
murayama = np.array([   # Temperature (°C), period (h), amplitude (peak-to-trough phosphorylated KaiC fraction)
    [19.55, 28.58, 0.017], [20.55, 27.88, 0.039], [21.24, 27.73, 0.062], [22.13, 27.09, 0.076],
    [23.03, 26.86, 0.095], [23.92, 26.53, 0.113], [24.82, 26.43, 0.120], [25.61, 26.34, 0.138],
    [27.40, 27.12, 0.147], [28.30, 26.46, 0.162], [29.91, 26.37, 0.185]])
```

### A Hopf bifurcation in the model

Looking back at @fig-strategies-temp in Section 7, the cancellation strategy stops oscillating on the cold side. Let us investigate how this happens.

When oscillation stops, the concentrations of the phosphorylation states settle to constant values: a steady state of the differential equations. A small displacement from that state evolves as $e^{\lambda t}$, where $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of the Jacobian at the steady state. If its real part is negative, the displacement decays and the steady state is stable. If the real part is positive, the displacement grows and oscillation emerges. A Hopf bifurcation occurs when the real parts of a pair of eigenvalues with nonzero imaginary parts change sign from negative to positive as a parameter such as temperature varies. Near the bifurcation, the emerging oscillation's period can be predicted from the imaginary part as $2\pi / \mathrm{Im}\,\lambda$.

```{python}
#| label: hopf
from scipy.optimize import fsolve

def f1(x, q):
    return rhs(np.asarray(x).reshape(3, 1), q).ravel()

def jacobian(x, q, h=1e-7):
    J = np.zeros((3, 3))
    f0 = f1(x, q)
    for j in range(3):
        xx = np.array(x, float); xx[j] += h
        J[:, j] = (f1(xx, q) - f0) / h
    return J

def fixed_point(q):
    x = fsolve(lambda x: f1(x, q), [0.8, 0.45, 0.57], xtol=1e-13)
    assert np.linalg.norm(f1(x, q)) < 1e-9
    return x

E_B = STRATEGIES["B"]
T_grid = np.round(np.arange(21.0, 30.01, 0.25), 2)
lam = []
for T in T_grid:
    q = at_temperature(p0, T, E_B)
    ev = np.linalg.eigvals(jacobian(fixed_point(q), q))
    lam.append(ev[np.argmax(ev.real)])
lam = np.array(lam)
T_c = np.interp(0.0, lam.real, T_grid)          # Temperature at which the real part crosses zero

# Amplitude and period just above the bifurcation (integrate longer because convergence is slow)
T_fine = np.round(np.arange(24.30, 25.01, 0.02), 2)
per_fine, amp_fine = period_amp([at_temperature(p0, T, E_B) for T in T_fine],
                                t_end=8000, t_skip=7000, dt=0.02)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-hopf
#| fig-cap: "The low-temperature Hopf bifurcation in the cancellation strategy. Left: real part of the steady-state eigenvalues. Middle: amplitude near the bifurcation. Right: period near the bifurcation and the period predicted from the imaginary part of the eigenvalue, $2\\pi/\\mathrm{Im}\\,\\lambda$. The dashed line marks the bifurcation."
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Figure code"
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3)
ax[0].plot(T_grid, lam.real, color=ORANGE)
ax[0].axhline(0, color=INK2, lw=0.8)
ax[0].set(xlabel="Temperature (°C)", ylabel="Largest eigenvalue real part (1/h)")
ax[1].plot(T_fine, amp_fine, "o", color=ORANGE, ms=4)
ax[1].set(xlabel="Temperature (°C)", ylabel="Amplitude (µM)")
ax[2].plot(T_fine, per_fine, "o", color=ORANGE, ms=4, label="Simulation")
ax[2].plot(T_grid, 2 * np.pi / np.abs(lam.imag), color=INK2, lw=1, label="2π / Im λ")
ax[2].set(xlim=(23, 26), ylim=(20, 24), xlabel="Temperature (°C)", ylabel="Period (h)")
ax[2].legend(fontsize=9)
for a in ax:
    a.axvline(T_c, color=MUTED, ls="--", lw=1)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

In the left panel of @fig-hopf, the real part of the eigenvalue crosses zero at `{python} f"{T_c:.2f}"` °C. As shown on the right, the period of the oscillation emerging just above the bifurcation is finite, approximately `{python} f"{np.nanmean(per_fine[:8]):.0f}"` hours, and agrees well with the prediction from the imaginary part. Oscillation in the model thus also stops through a Hopf bifurcation.

The amplitude behaves differently from the experiments, however. Immediately above a Hopf bifurcation, the amplitude should grow in proportion to the square root of the distance from the bifurcation. It does so in the model, but only over a range of approximately 0.1 °C. The amplitude rises sharply after crossing the bifurcation and levels off when it reaches the boundary at which S sequesters all KaiA, the dashed line in @fig-phase. This is a consequence of the sharp sequestration switch in @eq-freeA. In the experiments, amplitude declined gradually over a range of about 10 °C. We return to this discrepancy in Section 10.

The uniformly insensitive strategy, meanwhile, stops near `{python} f"{sweep['A']['lo']:.1f}"` °C, far below the experimental value of about 19 °C. When all reactions are temperature-insensitive, cooling barely changes the ratios between their rates, so oscillations are difficult to extinguish.

### Compensation weakens near the bifurcation

Temperature compensation itself also weakens near the bifurcation. We recalculate the control coefficients at different temperatures for the cancellation strategy (@tbl-cc-temperature).

```{python}
#| label: tbl-cc-temperature
#| tbl-cap: "Period and control coefficients at different temperatures for the cancellation strategy. The ledger is $\\sum_i C_i E_i$ (kJ/mol). The rightmost column gives the fraction of each cycle during which all KaiA is sequestered."
from IPython.display import Markdown
T_tbl = (24.6, 25.0, 27.5, 30.0, 32.5, 35.0, 36.5)
# Fraction of time with all KaiA sequestered (free KaiA = 0); integrate longer near the bifurcation, where relaxation is slow
t_sq, y_sq = integrate(stack([at_temperature(p0, T, E_B) for T in T_tbl]), 9000, dt=0.01, record_every=2)
S_sq = y_sq[t_sq > 7000][:, 2, :]
seq_frac = {T: np.mean(p0["KAIA"] - 2 * S_sq[:, j] <= 0) for j, T in enumerate(T_tbl)}
lines = ["| Temperature (°C) | Period (h) | C (S→ST) | C (ST→S, no KaiA) | ΣC | Ledger | Fraction of time with KaiA sequestered |",
         "|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|"]
for T in T_tbl:
    q = at_temperature(p0, T, E_B)
    CT = control_coeffs(q, RATE_NAMES)
    tau_T = period_amp([q])[0][0]
    ledger = sum(CT[n] * E_B[n] for n in RATE_NAMES)
    lines.append(f"| {T} | {tau_T:.2f} | {CT['SD_b']:+.2f} | {CT['DS_f']:+.2f} | "
                 f"{sum(CT.values()):+.3f} | {ledger:+.1f} | {seq_frac[T] * 100:.0f}% |")
Markdown("\n".join(lines))
```

The S → ST control coefficient, `{python} f"{C['SD_b']:+.2f}"` at 30 °C, becomes smaller near the bifurcation, tipping the ledger toward negative values. At the same time, the fraction of each cycle during which all KaiA is sequestered decreases, from `{python} f"{seq_frac[30.0] * 100:.0f}"`% at 30 °C to `{python} f"{seq_frac[24.6] * 100:.0f}"`% at 24.6 °C, as shown in the last column. In Section 6, S → ST lengthened the period by extending both the free-KaiA and sequestered-KaiA phases. As the phase in which the switch is active becomes shorter, this effect weakens. The diminished influence of period-lengthening reactions near the bifurcation agrees with Fu and colleagues' findings in general oscillator models [@fu2024]. At high temperatures, conversely, the control coefficient becomes too large, the ledger turns positive, and the period rises sharply. Balancing the ledger at 30 °C does not prevent the control coefficients themselves from changing with temperature elsewhere. The summation theorem, ΣC = −1, nevertheless holds at every temperature. Its somewhat larger deviation at 24.6 °C, very close to the bifurcation, reflects the long settling time and resulting numerical error in the period.

The experiments show a similar trend. In Murayama and colleagues' data, the period increases from `{python} f"{murayama[-1, 1]:.1f}"` hours at `{python} f"{murayama[-1, 0]:.1f}"` °C to `{python} f"{murayama[0, 1]:.1f}"` hours at `{python} f"{murayama[0, 0]:.1f}"` °C, just before oscillation disappears: an increase of approximately `{python} f"{(murayama[0, 1] / murayama[-1, 1] - 1) * 100:.0f}"`%. This is small compared with the reduction of amplitude to almost zero, and differs from a SNIC bifurcation, in which the period diverges. It is nevertheless consistent with the prediction that compensation weakens near the bifurcation.

### Can the clock entrain to temperature cycles?

In Section 1, we noted the apparent contradiction between temperature compensation and entrainment. A clock must sense temperature to entrain to a temperature cycle. Can our two temperature-compensated strategies do so?

Entrainment depends strongly on the difference between the clock's natural period and the temperature cycle's period. From this point on, we therefore scale all model rate constants down by the same factor to match the 23.1-hour period at 30 °C measured in vitro by Yoshida and colleagues [@yoshida2009]. This only rescales time and does not affect temperature dependence. We then impose a sinusoidal, 24-hour temperature cycle centered on 30 °C with an amplitude of ±ΔT and examine whether the oscillation period locks to 24 hours.

```{python}
#| label: forced
p_ref = {**p0, **{n: p0[n] * tau0 / 23.1 for n in RATE_NAMES}}     # Set the period at 30 °C to 23.1 h

def run_forced(p, E_rows, temp_fun, t_end=2400.0, t_skip=1400.0):
    """Integrate N parameter sets with time-varying temperature; return each set's mean period and variation.
    E_rows contains (N, 9) activation energies; temp_fun(t) returns an array of temperatures (°C) for the sets."""
    E_rows = np.asarray(E_rows, float)
    N = len(E_rows)
    base = {k: np.full(N, v) for k, v in p.items()}
    T0K = T_REF + 273.15
    def params_at(t):
        TK = temp_fun(t) + 273.15
        fac = np.exp(-(E_rows / R_GAS) * (1.0 / TK[:, None] - 1.0 / T0K))
        q = dict(base)
        for i, n in enumerate(RATE_NAMES):
            q[n] = p[n] * fac[:, i]
        return q
    t, y = integrate(base, t_end, dt=0.01, forcing=params_at, record_every=10)
    m = t >= t_skip
    Ptot = y[m].sum(axis=1)
    stats = []
    for j in range(N):
        d = np.diff(crossing_times(t[m], Ptot[:, j]))
        stats.append((d.mean(), d.std()) if len(d) >= 3 else (np.nan, np.nan))
    return np.array(stats), t, y

def is_locked(stat, T_cycle):
    return abs(stat[0] - T_cycle) < 0.05 and stat[1] < 0.05

def sine_entrainment(keys, dTs=(1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 5.0), t_end=3000.0, t_skip=2000.0):
    members = [(k, dT) for k in keys for dT in dTs]
    amp_arr = np.array([dT for _, dT in members])
    stats, t, y = run_forced(p_ref, [[STRATEGIES[k][n] for n in RATE_NAMES] for k, _ in members],
                             lambda t: 30.0 + amp_arr * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t / 24.0), t_end, t_skip)
    min_lock = {k: min([dT for (kk, dT), s in zip(members, stats) if kk == k and is_locked(s, 24.0)],
                       default=np.nan) for k in keys}
    return min_lock, members, t, y

min_lock, members_sine, t_sine, y_sine = sine_entrainment(("A", "B"))
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-entrain
#| fig-cap: "Total phosphorylated KaiC in the uniformly insensitive strategy (blue) and cancellation strategy (orange), subjected to a 24-hour temperature cycle of 30 ± 2 °C. Dotted lines mark 24-hour intervals."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Figure code"
w = t_sine >= t_sine[-1] - 24 * 6
tt = t_sine[w] - t_sine[w][0]
fig, (axT, axP) = plt.subplots(2, 1, sharex=True, gridspec_kw=dict(height_ratios=[1, 3]))
axT.plot(tt, 30 + 2 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t_sine[w] / 24), color=MUTED, lw=1.2)
axT.set_ylabel("Temperature (°C)")
for key in ("A", "B"):
    j = members_sine.index((key, 2.0))
    axP.plot(tt, y_sine[w][:, :, j].sum(axis=1), color=COLORS[key], label=NAMES[key])
for d in range(7):
    for a in (axT, axP):
        a.axvline(24 * d, color=MUTED, lw=0.6, ls=":")
axP.set(xlabel="Time (h)", ylabel="T+ST+S (µM)", ylim=(0.45, 2.45))
axP.legend(loc="lower left", ncol=2, fontsize=9)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The cancellation strategy locks to 24 hours under a small temperature cycle of ±`{python} f"{min_lock['B']:.0f}"` °C, with peaks recurring at the same time each day. The uniformly insensitive strategy, however, does not entrain until the temperature amplitude reaches ±`{python} f"{min_lock['A']:.0f}"` °C. In @fig-entrain, its blue curve at ±2 °C drifts relative to the 24-hour grid each day. Temperature-compensated clocks have been shown, in principle, to entrain to temperature cycles near their natural period [@bodenstein2012]. But a less temperature-sensitive clock is harder to entrain.

Why can a clock entrain to temperature cycles when its period is temperature-compensated? @fig-limitcycles overlays the limit cycles at 28 and 32 °C. In the uniformly insensitive strategy, the two nearly coincide. In the cancellation strategy, their sizes and positions differ even though their periods are almost identical. When temperature changes, the clock's state is left slightly off the limit cycle at the new temperature and then relaxes toward it. Its phase shifts during this relaxation. The time needed to complete a cycle may remain constant while the orbit itself moves with temperature. This is one way temperature compensation and entrainment can coexist. In the introduction to a recent preprint, which has not yet undergone peer review, Liu and colleagues likewise describe how temperature-dependent changes in the size and position of a limit cycle, with little change in its period, permit phase shifts in response to temperature changes, citing earlier work [@yoshida2009; @francois2012; @liu2026]. Several clock models, including a KaiC model, show that the very mechanism compensating the period moves the limit cycle and thereby produces phase shifts: period robustness and phase plasticity are two sides of the same relationship [@hatakeyama2015]. This is not the only mechanism for a phase shift, however. Even if the orbit's shape is unchanged, temperature can alter which parts are traversed quickly and which slowly, causing a phase shift at a temperature change. Other work shows that such waveform distortions affect both temperature compensation and the range of entrainment [@gibo2025]. François and colleagues also note that when period compensation relies on balancing many reactions, mean clock-protein levels vary with temperature, so the limit cycle's shape should vary as well [@francois2012].

```{python}
#| label: fig-limitcycles
#| fig-cap: "Limit cycles at 28 °C (solid) and 32 °C (dashed). Left: uniformly insensitive strategy. Right: cancellation strategy. Both strategies have nearly constant periods, but the position and size of the orbit change with temperature in the cancellation strategy."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Figure code"
def plot_limitcycles(ax, key):
    qs = [at_temperature(p0, T, STRATEGIES[key]) for T in (28.0, 32.0)]
    tl, yl = integrate(stack(qs), 600, dt=0.01, record_every=5)
    pers = period_amp_from(tl, yl, 300)[0]
    for j, (ls, T) in enumerate((("-", 28), ("--", 32))):
        one = tl >= tl[-1] - pers[j]                       # Plot only the final cycle
        yy = yl[one][:, :, j]
        ax.plot(yy[:, 2], yy.sum(axis=1), linestyle=ls, color=COLORS[key], lw=1.6,
                label=f"{T} °C (period {pers[j]:.1f} h)")
    ax.set(xlim=(0.3, 0.9), ylim=(0.75, 2.45), xlabel="S-state KaiC (µM)")
    ax.set_title(NAMES[key], fontsize=10.5, loc="left")
    ax.legend(fontsize=8.5, loc="upper right")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2)
for ax, key in zip(axes, ("A", "B")):
    plot_limitcycles(ax, key)
axes[0].set_ylabel("T+ST+S (µM)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The actual in vitro clock also entrains to temperature cycles. Yoshida and colleagues showed that it entrains to cycles alternating between 30 and 45 °C, and that each upward or downward temperature step produces a discrete phase shift whose size depends on the phase at which the step occurs [@yoshida2009]. The period stays unchanged, while phase shifts occur at the moments of temperature change—the same mechanism illustrated by the model. Another model focused on sequestration feedback also discusses how temperature-dependent sequestration of KaiA and KaiB can support both compensation and temperature entrainment [@brettschneider2010].

The strengths and weaknesses of the two strategies are now opposites. The uniformly insensitive strategy operates over a broad temperature range and withstands mutations, but does not stop at the observed low temperatures and is difficult to entrain. The cancellation strategy stops at low temperature and entrains readily, but operates only over a narrow temperature range and is vulnerable to mutations. Are temperature insensitivity and temperature sensing incompatible after all?

@fig-limitcycles offers a clue. One expression of temperature sensing was a change in the shape or position of the limit cycle without a change in period. We should therefore be able to construct ledgers for the limit cycle's shape and for temperature-induced phase shifts, just as we did for the period.

## Ledgers for amplitude and phase response {#sec-amplitude}

### Amplitude control coefficients

Many quantities describe the shape of a limit cycle. Here we use the amplitude $A$, defined as the peak-to-trough difference in total phosphorylated KaiC, T+ST+S. Analogously to the period, we define an amplitude control coefficient:

$$
C^{A}_i = \frac{\partial \ln A}{\partial \ln k_i}
$$ {#eq-cca}

This measures the fractional change in amplitude caused by a fractional change in a rate constant.

Amplitude control coefficients also obey a summation theorem. Scaling all rate constants by the same factor fast-forwards the clock. Doing so does not change how high or low the concentration of each phosphorylation state reaches; only the time scale changes. The amplitude is therefore unchanged, giving

$$
\sum_i C^{A}_i = 0
$$ {#eq-sum-a}

Whereas the right-hand side of the period summation theorem, @eq-sum, is −1, the amplitude summation theorem has a right-hand side of 0. Both were previously derived in metabolic control analysis of oscillations [@kholodenko1997].

The temperature dependence of amplitude can also be written in the same form as @eq-dlntau:

$$
\frac{d \ln A}{d T} = \frac{1}{RT^{2}} \sum_i C^{A}_i E_i
$$ {#eq-dlnA}

If the period ledger $\sum_i C_i E_i$ is zero, the period does not change with temperature. If the amplitude ledger $\sum_i C^A_i E_i$ is nonzero, amplitude does change. These are distinct ledgers, so it should be possible to keep one balanced while leaving the other unbalanced.

The amplitude summation theorem yields another useful result. Using @eq-sum-a, we can rewrite the amplitude ledger in terms of deviations from the mean activation energy $\bar{E}$:

$$
\sum_i C^{A}_i E_i = \sum_i C^{A}_i \left(E_i - \bar{E}\right)
$$ {#eq-amp-dev}

Because $\sum_i C^A_i = 0$, this equality holds for any constant in place of $\bar{E}$, not just the mean. What matters is how activation energies and amplitude control coefficients correlate across reactions. If every reaction has the same activation energy, the right-hand side is zero and amplitude is temperature-independent. For amplitude to increase with temperature, activation energies must vary across reactions, with a tendency for amplitude-increasing reactions, $C^A_i > 0$, to have larger activation energies. Observing a temperature-dependent amplitude in a temperature-compensated clock is thus itself evidence that its reactions do not all have the same activation energy.

This argument assumes that temperature changes only rate constants. If equilibrium constants such as $K_{1/2}$ also vary with temperature, their contributions enter the amplitude ledger as well. More precisely, a temperature-dependent amplitude means that temperature does more than uniformly fast-forward the whole clock. It is this assumption of uniform fast-forwarding that the observation directly rules out. It does not rule out mechanisms centered on temperature-insensitive reactions: even small differences in activation energy can produce large amplitude changes if the clock is near a bifurcation, as we will see shortly.

Several temperature-compensated clocks exhibit quantities that vary with temperature: FRQ protein abundance in *Neurospora crassa* [@liu1998], the expression amplitudes of some clock genes in cultured rat cells [@kurosawa2017], and the amplitude of KaiABC phosphorylation rhythms [@murayama2017]. Theory has also predicted increasing amplitude with temperature in compensated oscillators [@ruoff2003]. Here, we express this behavior through control coefficients alongside the period ledger.

```{python}
#| label: amplitude-coeffs
def amplitude_coeffs(p, names, h=0.01):
    """Control coefficients of amplitude (peak-to-trough T+ST+S); record finely to locate extrema accurately."""
    plist = []
    for n in names:
        for s in (+1, -1):
            q = dict(p)
            q[n] = p[n] * np.exp(s * h)
            plist.append(q)
    t, y = integrate(stack(plist), 1000, dt=0.01, record_every=1)
    _, amp = period_amp_from(t, y, 600)
    return {n: (np.log(amp[2 * i]) - np.log(amp[2 * i + 1])) / (2 * h) for i, n in enumerate(names)}

CA_all = amplitude_coeffs(p0, RATE_NAMES + ["KHALF"])
CA = {n: CA_all[n] for n in RATE_NAMES}
CA_sum = sum(CA.values())
amp_ledger = {key: sum(CA[n] * STRATEGIES[key][n] for n in RATE_NAMES) for key in ("A", "B")}

# Convert the amplitude increase in Murayama et al.'s data (25–30 °C) to a ledger value
i25, i30m = np.argmin(abs(murayama[:, 0] - 25)), np.argmin(abs(murayama[:, 0] - 30))
slope_exp = np.log(murayama[i30m, 2] / murayama[i25, 2]) / (murayama[i30m, 0] - murayama[i25, 0])
ledger_exp = slope_exp * R_GAS * (T_REF + 273.15) ** 2

# Estimate the Hopf temperature by fitting amplitude squared as a linear function of temperature (at or below 26 °C)
low = murayama[:, 0] < 26
sl, ic = np.polyfit(murayama[low, 0], murayama[low, 2] ** 2, 1)
Tc_fit = -ic / sl
hopf_ledger = R_GAS * (27.5 + 273.15) ** 2 / (2 * (27.5 - Tc_fit))
```

Numerically, the amplitude control coefficients of the nine rate constants sum to `{python} f"{round(CA_sum, 3) + 0.0:.3f}"`, confirming @eq-sum-a.

This equation explains why the uniformly insensitive strategy sensed temperature so weakly. If every reaction has the same activation energy $E_0$, the amplitude ledger is $E_0 \sum_i C^A_i = 0$, and amplitude is temperature-independent. In our uniformly insensitive strategy, S → ST has a slightly different activation energy, so the ledger is not exactly zero, but its value is small: `{python} f"{amp_ledger['A']:.0f}"` kJ/mol. The cancellation strategy's amplitude ledger is `{python} f"{amp_ledger['B']:.0f}"` kJ/mol. For comparison, in Murayama and colleagues' data, amplitude increases by approximately `{python} f"{(np.exp(slope_exp) - 1) * 100:.0f}"`% per °C between 25 and 30 °C. Through @eq-dlnA, this corresponds to a ledger value of about `{python} f"{ledger_exp:.0f}"` kJ/mol. The real clock's amplitude ledger is clearly unbalanced. In terms of @eq-amp-dev, amplitude-increasing reactions have activation energies appreciably above the mean.

This value needs care in interpretation, however. In Murayama and colleagues' data, amplitude squared decreases approximately linearly as temperature falls. This is the behavior expected just above a Hopf bifurcation, where $d\ln A/dT = 1/\{2(T - T_c)\}$ grows as the bifurcation temperature $T_c$ is approached. Fitting a line to amplitude squared gives $T_c$ ≈ `{python} f"{Tc_fit:.1f}"` °C. Evaluating this expression at 27.5 °C and converting to ledger units yields approximately `{python} f"{hopf_ledger:.0f}"` kJ/mol. The large experimental amplitude ledger also reflects the fact that 25–30 °C remains close to the bifurcation.

### The phase-response ledger

The amplitude ledger tells us how the size of the oscillation changes with temperature and whether it tends to disappear upon cooling. But amplitude does not directly determine whether the clock entrains to a temperature cycle. What matters is how much its phase shifts after a small temperature change: the *phase response*. Even if amplitude changes, entrainment does not occur if the clock's rate of advance changes equally at every phase.

For a clock at phase $\phi$, with one cycle represented by 0–2π, let $g_i(\phi)$ describe the change in phase velocity per change in the logarithm of reaction $i$'s rate constant. Raising temperature by $\delta T$ changes each log rate constant by $E_i\,\delta T / RT^2$, so the phase response to temperature is

$$
\Gamma_T(\phi) = \frac{1}{RT^{2}} \sum_i E_i\, g_i(\phi)
$$ {#eq-gamma}

This has the same ledger form as the period and amplitude equations, but now the ledger has a value at every phase.

The fast-forwarding argument applies again. Increasing every rate constant by the same factor simply moves the clock around the same orbit faster by that factor, so phase velocity increases proportionally at every phase. Thus, $\sum_i g_i(\phi)$ is independent of phase and equals the angular frequency $\omega = 2\pi/\tau$. Also, the cycle average of $g_i$ is $-\omega C_i$, because it represents the change in period caused by changing that rate constant. This relationship between phase responses accumulated over a cycle and the resulting period change is established in oscillator sensitivity analysis [@gunawan2006; @taylor2008]. Together, these facts give

$$
\Gamma_T(\phi) = -\frac{\omega}{RT^{2}} \sum_i C_i E_i + \frac{1}{RT^{2}} \sum_i \left(E_i - \bar{E}\right)\left(g_i(\phi) + \omega C_i\right)
$$ {#eq-gamma-split}

The first term is the period ledger itself, a constant independent of phase. It vanishes when the period is compensated. Only the second term varies with phase, and it depends solely on deviations $E_i - \bar{E}$ from the mean activation energy.

This leads to a conclusion: **if temperature merely rescales time, the clock cannot entrain to temperature cycles.** Temperature changes then alter the clock's rate of advance by the same amount at every phase, providing no restoring effect that aligns phases. A clock with identical activation energies, such as the all-50-kJ/mol clock in Section 5, is an example. As with amplitude, however, this conclusion rules out only the assumption that temperature acts solely through uniform fast-forwarding. In a clock whose period is compensated but whose dynamics still respond to temperature, activation energies necessarily vary. The important question is therefore not whether they vary, but which reactions carry that variation and how.

We now calculate $g_i(\phi)$ numerically. At each phase of the oscillation, we perturb one rate constant slightly for a short interval, 30 minutes, and measure the phase shift after sufficient time has passed.

```{python}
#| label: prc
def phase_response(p, names, n_phase=64, eps=0.05, pulse=0.5):
    """Perturb each parameter by exp(±eps) for a duration pulse at each phase, and use the phase shift to estimate
    the reaction's phase response g_i(φ): change in phase velocity per unit ln k_i, in 1/h."""
    t, y = integrate(stack([p]), 1600, dt=0.01, record_every=1)
    Ptot = y[:, :, 0].sum(axis=1)
    keep = t > 1200
    level = Ptot[keep].mean()
    def up_cross(tt, PP):
        c = PP - level
        i = np.where((c[:-1] < 0) & (c[1:] >= 0))[0]
        return tt[i] - c[i] * (tt[i + 1] - tt[i]) / (c[i + 1] - c[i])
    tc = up_cross(t[keep], Ptot[keep])
    tau = np.diff(tc).mean()
    i0 = np.searchsorted(t, tc[0])                        # Phase 0: T+ST+S crosses its mean from below
    starts = [i0 + int(round(j * tau / n_phase / 0.01)) for j in range(n_phase)]
    cols = [(j, None, 0) for j in range(n_phase)] + \
           [(j, n, s) for j in range(n_phase) for n in names for s in (+1, -1)]
    base = {k: np.full(len(cols), v) for k, v in p.items()}
    pert = {k: v.copy() for k, v in base.items()}
    for c, (j, n, s) in enumerate(cols):
        if n is not None:
            pert[n][c] *= np.exp(s * eps)
    x0 = np.concatenate([y[starts[j], :, 0].reshape(3, 1) for j, _, _ in cols], axis=1)
    tt, yy = integrate(base, 6 * tau, dt=0.01, x0=x0, record_every=2,
                       forcing=lambda s: pert if s < pulse else base)
    PP = yy.sum(axis=1)
    first = []
    for c in range(len(cols)):
        cc = up_cross(tt, PP[:, c])
        first.append(cc[cc > 4 * tau][0])                 # First crossing after sufficient relaxation
    first = np.array(first)
    pos = {col: k for k, col in enumerate(cols)}
    wrap = lambda d: (d + tau / 2) % tau - tau / 2
    g = {}
    for n in names:
        adv = [wrap(first[pos[(j, None, 0)]] - first[pos[(j, n, +1)]])
               - wrap(first[pos[(j, None, 0)]] - first[pos[(j, n, -1)]]) for j in range(n_phase)]
        g[n] = np.array(adv) * (2 * np.pi / tau) / (2 * eps * pulse)
    return np.arange(n_phase) / n_phase * 2 * np.pi, tau, g

phi_g, tau_g, g_rate = phase_response(p_ref, RATE_NAMES)
omega_g = 2 * np.pi / tau_g
RT2 = R_GAS * (T_REF + 273.15) ** 2
sum_g = sum(g_rate.values()) / omega_g

def gamma_T(E):
    """Temperature phase response Γ_T(φ), per kelvin, in 1/h."""
    return sum(E[n] * g_rate[n] for n in RATE_NAMES) / RT2

def gamma_first_harmonic(E):
    """Magnitude of the fundamental harmonic of Γ_T."""
    G = gamma_T(E)
    return np.hypot(2 * np.mean(G * np.cos(phi_g)), 2 * np.mean(G * np.sin(phi_g)))
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-prc
#| fig-cap: "Left: phase response $g_i(\\phi)$ of each reaction at 30 °C: how much increasing a rate constant at a given phase speeds up the clock, normalized by the angular frequency ω. The black dashed line is the sum over all nine reactions. Right: temperature phase response $\\Gamma_T(\\phi)$: the percentage increase in clock speed caused by a 1 °C temperature increase at each phase. Phase 0 on the horizontal axis is the upward crossing of the mean total phosphorylated KaiC."
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Figure code"
hours = phi_g / (2 * np.pi) * tau_g
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2)
for n in RATE_NAMES:
    color = ORANGE if n == "SD_b" else (BLUE if n == "DS_f" else (AQUA if n == "UT_b" else GRID))
    lw = 2.0 if color != GRID else 1.2
    ax[0].plot(hours, g_rate[n] / omega_g, color=color, lw=lw,
               label=LABELS[n] if color != GRID else None, zorder=3 if color != GRID else 2)
ax[0].plot(hours, sum_g, color=INK2, ls="--", lw=1.4, label="Sum of all 9")
ax[0].set(xlabel="Phase (h)", ylabel="$g_i(\\phi)$ / ω")
ax[0].legend(fontsize=8.5, loc="upper right")
E_uniform = {n: 50.0 for n in RATE_NAMES}
for key, E, color, lab in (("U", E_uniform, MUTED, "All 50 kJ/mol (uncompensated)"),
                            ("A", STRATEGIES["A"], COLORS["A"], NAMES["A"]),
                            ("B", STRATEGIES["B"], COLORS["B"], NAMES["B"])):
    ax[1].plot(hours, gamma_T(E) / omega_g * 100, color=color, label=lab)
ax[1].axhline(0, color=INK2, lw=0.8)
ax[1].set(xlabel="Phase (h)", ylabel="$\\Gamma_T(\\phi)$ (%/°C)")
ax[1].legend(fontsize=8.5, loc="lower left")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

In the left panel of @fig-prc, the individual reaction responses vary strongly with phase, but their sum is 1 at every phase, ranging numerically from `{python} f"{sum_g.min():.3f}"` to `{python} f"{sum_g.max():.3f}"` in the plotted normalization. This is exactly what the fast-forwarding argument predicts.

The right panel shows the temperature phase response. In the all-50-kJ/mol clock, $\Gamma_T$ is nearly constant across phases, approximately `{python} f"{np.mean(gamma_T(E_uniform)) / omega_g * 100:.1f}"`%/°C. Warming simply speeds up the clock equally at every phase, so it cannot align its phase to a temperature cycle. In the compensated uniformly insensitive and cancellation strategies, the mean response is zero and the response takes positive and negative values across the cycle. Warming advances the clock at some phases and delays it at others. This phase dependence provides the restoring effect needed for entrainment. Its excursion is much larger in the cancellation strategy, consistent with the stronger entrainment observed in Section 8.

We can now separate two aspects of "sensing temperature": amplitude changes are described by the amplitude ledger, and entrainment by the phase-response ledger. The amplitude ledger is only a local slope at 30 °C, however. For a gradual Hopf bifurcation like that observed experimentally, it is connected to the temperature at which oscillation stops through the relation $1/\{2(T - T_c)\}$ discussed above. In this model, with its sharp KaiA sequestration switch, amplitude collapses so abruptly that its slope at 30 °C cannot predict the stopping temperature. In both ledgers, what matters is the deviation of activation energies from their mean, $E_i - \bar{E}$.

### Where should temperature-sensitive reactions be placed?

How can we unbalance the amplitude ledger while keeping the period ledger balanced? @fig-two-ledgers plots each reaction's period control coefficient against its amplitude control coefficient.

```{python}
#| label: fig-two-ledgers
#| fig-cap: "Period control coefficient (horizontal axis) and amplitude control coefficient (vertical axis) of each reaction at 30 °C. Orange marks S → ST (KaiA), which has a positive effect on both period and amplitude. Green marks U → T (KaiA), which strongly affects amplitude but barely affects period."
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 5
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Figure code"
offsets = {"UT_b": (8, 4), "TD_b": (-10, 8), "SD_b": (-8, -16), "US_b": (-10, -4), "TU_b": (8, -4),
           "DT_b": (8, 2), "TU_f": (8, 4), "DS_f": (8, -6), "SU_f": (0, -18), "KHALF": (8, -4)}
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.axhline(0, color=MUTED, lw=0.8)
ax.axvline(0, color=MUTED, lw=0.8)
for n in RATE_NAMES + ["KHALF"]:
    x, yv = C_all[n], CA_all[n]
    color = AQUA if n == "UT_b" else (ORANGE if n == "SD_b" else INK2)
    ax.plot(x, yv, "o", color=color, ms=8)
    ha = "right" if offsets[n][0] < 0 else ("center" if offsets[n][0] == 0 else "left")
    ax.annotate(LABELS.get(n, "K½ (binding constant)"), (x, yv), offsets[n], textcoords="offset points",
                fontsize=8.5, color=INK2, ha=ha)
ax.set(xlabel="Period control coefficient C", ylabel="Amplitude control coefficient C^A", xlim=(-1.45, 1.45), ylim=(-1.0, 1.1))
plt.show()
```

Three broad types of reaction emerge. Some, such as ST → S without KaiA, have negative effects on both period and amplitude. Others, such as S → ST, have positive effects on both. A third type, exemplified by KaiA-dependent U → T, has little effect on period, `{python} f"{C['UT_b']:+.2f}"`, but a strong effect on amplitude, `{python} f"{CA['UT_b']:+.2f}"`. The amplitude increase caused by a period-lengthening reaction such as S → ST follows the mechanism in Section 6: it lengthens the period by increasing the oscillatory excursion.

Once the period ledger is balanced, how we unbalance the amplitude ledger depends on where we place temperature-sensitive reactions—those with large activation energies—in this plot. Broadly, there are three strategies. This is a conceptual classification for organizing the discussion, not an established taxonomy in the field. Actual clocks may combine several strategies, and the description can depend on the level at which we examine them. For example, if opposing temperature dependences within KaiC cancel to make ATPase activity insensitive, a cancellation mechanism within the molecule appears as a temperature-insensitive component at the level of the whole clock.

The first strategy makes every reaction temperature-insensitive, as in the uniformly insensitive strategy of Section 7. Both ledgers remain close to zero, and the clock barely senses temperature.

The second makes a reaction with positive effects on both period and amplitude, such as S → ST in the upper right, temperature-sensitive. Warming accelerates S → ST, increasing the excursion and lengthening the period. This offsets the shortening caused by acceleration of other reactions. Period compensation and amplitude growth arise from the same reaction, so we call this the *coupled strategy*. The cancellation strategy of Section 7 was an extreme coupled case in which every reaction was temperature-sensitive. The idea that increasing amplitude helps preserve period in compensated oscillators has a long history [@ruoff2003]. One study argued from mathematical models that maintaining the period requires gene-expression amplitude to increase with temperature, and demonstrated such increases for some clock genes in cultured rat cells [@kurosawa2017]. In the KaiABC clock as well, temperature dependence of the amplitude-setting switch has been reported to contribute to period compensation [@liu2026].

The third strategy makes a reaction such as U → T temperature-sensitive: one that has little influence on period but a strong influence on amplitude. Increasing its activation energy barely changes the period ledger while unbalancing the amplitude ledger. Reactions that control period remain temperature-insensitive, while reactions with little effect on period sense temperature. We call this the *division-of-labor strategy*. This idea also has precedents. François and colleagues considered oscillator models in which temperature enters only a few terms, while the rest are temperature-independent. In such clocks, changing temperature merely expands or contracts the limit cycle, and the shape of the phase-response curve is also temperature-independent [@francois2012]. Kidd and colleagues developed this into a "pathway model," in which each period-determining process is individually temperature-compensated and temperature is sensed through a dedicated pathway connected to the clock [@kidd2015].

We construct families of coupled and division-of-labor strategies by varying one reaction's activation energy. For the coupled family, we start from the uniformly insensitive strategy, increase the S → ST activation energy, and balance the period ledger by adjusting ST → S without KaiA. These are the only two strongly temperature-sensitive reactions. For the division-of-labor family, we increase the U → T activation energy and balance the ledger through S → ST as before.

```{python}
#| label: families
def coupled_E(E_sd, E_base=10.0):
    """Set the S→ST activation energy to E_sd and balance the period ledger at 30 °C using ST→S (no KaiA)."""
    E = {n: E_base for n in RATE_NAMES}
    E["SD_b"] = E_sd
    E["DS_f"] = -sum(C[n] * E[n] for n in RATE_NAMES if n != "DS_f") / C["DS_f"]
    return E

fam_C = [20.0, 35.0, 50.0, 70.0]      # S→ST (20 kJ/mol is nearly the uniformly insensitive strategy)
fam_R = [10.0, 40.0, 70.0, 100.0]     # U→T (10 kJ/mol is exactly the uniformly insensitive strategy)
E_fams = [coupled_E(e) for e in fam_C] + [balance_E(10.0, e) for e in fam_R]
temps_f = np.arange(0.0, 50.01, 0.5)
per_f, amp_f = period_amp([at_temperature(p0, T, E) for E in E_fams for T in temps_f], t_end=2000, t_skip=1300)
per_f = per_f.reshape(len(E_fams), -1)
amp_f = amp_f.reshape(len(E_fams), -1)
i30f = np.argmin(abs(temps_f - 30))
stop_f = [temps_f[np.isfinite(r)].min() for r in per_f]
aled_f = [sum(CA[n] * E[n] for n in RATE_NAMES) for E in E_fams]
band = (temps_f >= 25) & (temps_f <= 45)
flat_f = max(np.nanmax(np.abs(r[band] / r[i30f] - 1)) for r in per_f)
nC = len(fam_C)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-families
#| fig-cap: "Temperature dependence of period (left) and amplitude (right) in the coupled strategy (top, varying the S → ST activation energy) and division-of-labor strategy (bottom, varying the U → T activation energy). Both are normalized to their values at 30 °C. Darker colors indicate higher activation energies. Parentheses in the legends give the amplitude ledger."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Figure code"
oranges = ["#f6c5a8", "#f19a6c", "#eb6834", "#a3401a"]
greens = ["#a8dcc6", "#5fc29c", "#1baf7a", "#0d6e4b"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 2, sharex=True)
for row, (fam, cols, name, off) in enumerate(((fam_C, oranges, "S→ST", 0), (fam_R, greens, "U→T", nC))):
    for k, (e, c) in enumerate(zip(fam, cols)):
        j = off + k
        lab = f"{name}: {e:.0f} kJ/mol ({aled_f[j]:.0f})"
        ax[row, 0].plot(temps_f, per_f[j] / per_f[j, i30f], color=c, label=lab)
        ax[row, 1].plot(temps_f, amp_f[j] / amp_f[j, i30f], color=c, label=lab)
    ax[row, 0].set(ylim=(0.9, 1.15), ylabel="Period / period at 30 °C")
    ax[row, 1].set(ylim=(-0.05, 2.0), ylabel="Amplitude / amplitude at 30 °C")
    ax[row, 0].legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper right")
    ax[row, 0].set_title(["Coupled", "Division of labor"][row], fontsize=10.5, loc="left")
for a in ax[1]:
    a.set_xlabel("Temperature (°C)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

In both families, period changes very little from 25 to 45 °C, deviating from its 30 °C value by at most `{python} f"{flat_f * 100:.1f}"`%, while amplitude changes substantially (@fig-families). Increasing the activation energy of the temperature-sensitive reaction makes the amplitude ledger larger and raises the temperature at which oscillations stop on cooling. The stopping temperatures are `{python} ", ".join(f"{v:.1f}" for v in stop_f[:nC])` °C in the coupled family and `{python} ", ".join(f"{v:.1f}" for v in stop_f[nC:])` °C in the division-of-labor family. Both can unbalance the amplitude ledger while keeping the period ledger balanced.

The difference is in how efficiently they do so. At the same activation energy of 70 kJ/mol, the amplitude ledger is `{python} f"{aled_f[fam_C.index(70.0)]:.0f}"` kJ/mol for the coupled strategy and `{python} f"{aled_f[nC + fam_R.index(70.0)]:.0f}"` kJ/mol for the division-of-labor strategy. In the coupled case, part of the amplitude-increasing effect of S → ST is canceled by the ST → S reaction used to balance the period; the latter's amplitude control coefficient is `{python} f"{CA['DS_f']:+.2f}"`.

## Comparing the three strategies with experiments {#sec-experiment}

Which strategy is closest to experiment? We use four experimental observations for comparison:

1. The in vitro rhythm disappears at approximately 19 °C and is undetectable at 18.6 °C or below [@murayama2017].
2. A stable rhythm persists at 45 °C, with almost the same period as at 30 °C: 23.4 and 23.3 hours in the same reaction mixture. 45 °C was the highest temperature at which a stable rhythm was observed [@yoshida2009].
3. The period Q~10~ between 25 and 35 °C is approximately 1.05–1.1 [@nakajima2005; @itomiwa2020].
4. The clock entrains to cycles alternating equally between 30 and 45 °C when their periods are 20–28 hours, but not at 16 or 32 hours [@yoshida2009].

Three caveats are needed before comparing them. First, experimental conditions differ. The period at 30 °C ranges from roughly 21 to 26 hours depending on protein preparation [@nakajima2005; @yoshida2009; @murayama2017]. Period Q~10~ also depends on KaiA concentration: it can be 1.05 under standard conditions but rises to 1.27–1.30 when KaiA is increased approximately threefold [@itomiwa2020]. We therefore compare periods and amplitudes relative to their values at 30 °C, focusing on differences between strategies rather than precise numerical agreement.

Second, some parameters have been tuned. We set the S → ST activation energy in the coupled strategy and the U → T activation energy in the division-of-labor strategy to 70 kJ/mol, corresponding to a reaction-rate Q~10~ of approximately `{python} f"{q10_rate(70):.1f}"`. At this value, both strategies reproduce the experimental pattern of entrainment to 30/45 °C cycles. That pattern therefore cannot serve to distinguish them.

Third, the period at 45 °C also does not distinguish the strategies. Since each period ledger is balanced at 30 °C, their periods change relatively little even at 45 °C. Differences emerge in the temperature at which oscillations stop, the temperature dependence of amplitude, and the ease of entrainment to sinusoidal temperature cycles. As in Section 8, we use a model rescaled to a 23.1-hour period at 30 °C.

```{python}
#| label: compare
STRATEGIES["C"] = coupled_E(70.0)
STRATEGIES["R"] = balance_E(10.0, 70.0)
keys = ("A", "B", "C", "R")
iC, iR = keys.index("C"), keys.index("R")
temps_c = np.arange(10.0, 55.01, 0.5)
per_c, amp_c = period_amp([at_temperature(p_ref, T, STRATEGIES[k]) for k in keys for T in temps_c],
                          t_end=2400, t_skip=1600)
per_c = per_c.reshape(len(keys), -1)
amp_c = amp_c.reshape(len(keys), -1)
i30c = np.argmin(abs(temps_c - 30))

# Temperature cycles spending equal time at 30 °C and 45 °C (integrate longer to assess entrainment reliably)
cycle_T = [16.0, 20.0, 24.0, 28.0, 32.0]
mem = [(k, Tp) for k in keys for Tp in cycle_T]
Tp_arr = np.array([Tp for _, Tp in mem])
stats_sq, _, _ = run_forced(p_ref, [[STRATEGIES[k][n] for n in RATE_NAMES] for k, _ in mem],
                            lambda t: np.where(np.mod(t, Tp_arr) < Tp_arr / 2, 45.0, 30.0),
                            t_end=5000, t_skip=4000)
locked_sq = np.array([is_locked(s, Tp) for s, (_, Tp) in zip(stats_sq, mem)]).reshape(len(keys), -1)

min_lock.update(sine_entrainment(("C", "R"))[0])     # 24-hour sinusoid (A and B were computed in Section 8)
detune = abs(omega_g - 2 * np.pi / 24.0)             # Difference between the clock and temperature-cycle angular frequencies
pred_lock = {k: 2 * detune / gamma_first_harmonic(STRATEGIES[k]) for k in keys}   # Phase-response prediction
for k in ("C", "R"):
    mut[k] = mutation_test(p0, STRATEGIES[k])
    amp_ledger[k] = sum(CA[n] * STRATEGIES[k][n] for n in RATE_NAMES)

stop_c = {k: temps_c[np.isfinite(per_c[i])].min() for i, k in enumerate(keys)}
r45_c = {k: per_c[i, np.argmin(abs(temps_c - 45))] / per_c[i, i30c] for i, k in enumerate(keys)}
amp_at_stop = {k: amp_c[i, np.argmin(abs(temps_c - stop_c[k]))] / amp_c[i, i30c] for i, k in enumerate(keys)}
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-compare
#| tbl-colwidths: [24, 15, 15, 15, 15, 16]
#| tbl-cap: "Comparison of the four strategies with experiments; model periods at 30 °C are set to 23.1 hours. ○ indicates entrainment, and × indicates no entrainment. The cancellation strategy does not oscillate at 45 °C, so its ○ represents a response forced by temperature changes. Sinusoidal simulations test amplitudes of ±1, 2, 3, and 5 °C and report the smallest that produces entrainment. The mutant row gives the median $|\\ln Q_{10}|$ and the number that stop oscillating at 25 °C or 35 °C, using the same 20 mutants as in Section 7."
def at_Tc(i, T):
    return per_c[i, np.argmin(abs(temps_c - T))]
def osc_range(i):
    ok = temps_c[np.isfinite(per_c[i])]
    lo = f"≤{temps_c[0]:.0f}" if ok.min() <= temps_c[0] else f"{ok.min():.1f}"
    hi = f"≥{temps_c[-1]:.0f}" if ok.max() >= temps_c[-1] else f"{ok.max():.1f}"
    return f"{lo}–{hi}"
rows_tbl = {
    "Oscillating temperature range (°C)": [osc_range(i) for i in range(len(keys))] + ["Approx. 19–45"],
    "Amplitude ledger (kJ/mol)": [f"{amp_ledger[k]:.0f}" for k in keys] + [f"Approx. {ledger_exp:.0f}"],
    "Q10 (25–35 °C)": [f"{at_Tc(i, 25) / at_Tc(i, 35):.3f}" for i in range(len(keys))] + ["Approx. 1.05–1.1"],
    "Period ratio (45 °C / 30 °C)": [("—" if np.isnan(at_Tc(i, 45)) else f"{at_Tc(i, 45) / at_Tc(i, 30):.3f}") for i in range(len(keys))] + ["Approx. 1.00"],
    "Entrainment to 30/45 °C cycles (periods: 16, 20, 24, 28, 32 h)": [" ".join("○" if x else "×" for x in locked_sq[i]) for i in range(len(keys))] + ["× ○ ○ ○ ×"],
    "Minimum amplitude for entrainment to a 24-hour sinusoid (simulation)": [f"±{min_lock[k]:.0f} °C" for k in keys] + ["—"],
    "Same threshold, predicted from phase response": [f"±{pred_lock[k]:.1f} °C" for k in keys] + ["—"],
    "Mutants (median / number stopped)": [f"{mut[k]['med']:.3f} / {mut[k]['lost']}" for k in keys] + ["—"],
}
lines = ["| | " + " | ".join(NAMES[k] for k in keys) + " | Experiments |", "|:--|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|"]
for label, vals in rows_tbl.items():
    lines.append(f"| {label} | " + " | ".join(vals) + " |")
Markdown("\n".join(lines))
```

```{python}
ax[1].set(xlim=(10, 52), ylim=(-0.05, 1.7), xlabel="Temperature (°C)", ylabel="Amplitude / amplitude at 30 °C")
```
