
In @tbl-compare and @fig-vs-exp, the clearest distinction is the temperature at which oscillations stop. The uniformly insensitive strategy does not stop in the relevant low-temperature range. The cancellation, coupled, and division-of-labor strategies stop at `{python} f"{stop_c['B']:.1f}"`, `{python} f"{stop_c['C']:.1f}"`, and `{python} f"{stop_c['R']:.1f}"` °C, respectively. The division-of-labor strategy is closest to the experimental value of about 19 °C, but is still roughly 2 °C too high; experimentally, rhythms remain observable at 19.5–21 °C. Estimates of the bifurcation temperature do depend on the analysis, however. A reanalysis of Murayama and colleagues' data based on responses after cooling placed it at approximately 21.4 °C [@mihalcescu2025]. The difference between the division-of-labor and coupled strategies also shrinks with different tuning. As shown in Section 9, setting S → ST to 50 kJ/mol in the coupled strategy gives a stopping temperature of `{python} f"{stop_f[fam_C.index(50.0)]:.1f}"` °C, almost the same as in the division-of-labor strategy. The stopping temperature alone cannot distinguish these two. The cancellation strategy cannot sustain oscillations up to 45 °C; its period matching the 30/45 °C cycle is better interpreted as a response driven by temperature changes than as entrainment of a sustained oscillator.

None of the strategies reaches the experimentally estimated amplitude ledger of approximately `{python} f"{ledger_exp:.0f}"` kJ/mol. The cancellation strategy comes closest, at `{python} f"{amp_ledger['B']:.0f}"` kJ/mol, followed by the division-of-labor strategy at `{python} f"{amp_ledger['R']:.0f}"` kJ/mol and the coupled strategy at `{python} f"{amp_ledger['C']:.0f}"` kJ/mol. This ordering does not match the ordering of stopping temperatures. As cautioned in Section 9, this model's amplitude ledger at 30 °C cannot predict where oscillation stops. There is also a shared discrepancy in the shape of the amplitude curve. All three strategies that stop at low temperature collapse abruptly to zero from an amplitude still several tens of percent of the 30 °C value: `{python} f"{amp_at_stop['R'] * 100:.0f}"`% for the division-of-labor strategy and `{python} f"{amp_at_stop['C'] * 100:.0f}"`% for the coupled strategy. This reflects the sharp KaiA sequestration switch discussed in Section 8. Experimentally, amplitude approaches zero gradually near 19 °C. These two discrepancies—the undersized amplitude ledger and the abrupt collapse—share a cause. As discussed in Section 9, the large experimental ledger reflects a gradual amplitude decline approaching a Hopf bifurcation. The model's sharp sequestration switch leaves almost no such gradual regime, as seen in Section 8.

Entrainment to temperature cycles can be predicted from the phase response in Section 9. When the clock is driven by a temperature cycle of amplitude $\Delta T$ and angular frequency $\Omega$, the phase difference $\psi$ between clock and temperature cycle obeys, after averaging over a cycle,

$$
\frac{d\psi}{dt} = (\omega - \Omega) + \Delta T\, H(\psi)
$$ {#eq-locking}

Here, $H(\psi)$ is determined by the fundamental harmonic of $\Gamma_T$, the component with one period per cycle, and its amplitude is half the harmonic magnitude $|\Gamma_1|$. Entrainment requires a constant phase difference, so there must be a $\psi$ at which the right-hand side is zero. The minimum entraining amplitude is therefore $\Delta T_{\min} = 2|\omega - \Omega| / |\Gamma_1|$. As @tbl-compare shows, this prediction agrees well with the simulations. Moreover, although the amplitude ledgers of the uniformly insensitive and coupled strategies differ by about a factor of three—`{python} f"{amp_ledger['A']:.0f}"` and `{python} f"{amp_ledger['C']:.0f}"` kJ/mol—their ease of entrainment is almost identical, with predicted thresholds of ±`{python} f"{pred_lock['A']:.1f}"` and ±`{python} f"{pred_lock['C']:.1f}"` °C. Understanding entrainment requires the phase-response ledger, not the amplitude ledger.

Mutational robustness differs across strategies. The division-of-labor strategy is about as robust as the uniformly insensitive strategy, with a median $|\ln Q_{10}|$ of `{python} f"{mut['R']['med']:.3f}"`. The coupled strategy, at `{python} f"{mut['C']['med']:.3f}"`, lies between these and the cancellation strategy, at `{python} f"{mut['B']['med']:.3f}"`. The coupled strategy also has `{python} f"{mut['C']['lost']}"` mutants that lose oscillation, although its unmutated clock already stops below `{python} f"{stop_c['C']:.1f}"` °C, placing the 25 °C test near the boundary of its range. We do not have experimental values for this robustness comparison.

We next examine how the stopping temperature and entrainment pattern depend on the tuned parameters in the division-of-labor strategy. @tbl-param-scan varies the U → T activation energy and the activation energy $E_0$ of the temperature-insensitive part, which has so far been fixed at 10 kJ/mol.

```{python}
#| label: param-scan
E0_scan = [5.0, 10.0, 12.5, 15.0, 20.0]
sens_scan = [50.0, 60.0, 70.0]
combos = [(e0, es) for e0 in E0_scan for es in sens_scan]
temps_scan = np.concatenate([np.arange(17.0, 25.01, 0.5), [30.0, 45.0]])
per_scan, _ = period_amp([at_temperature(p_ref, T, balance_E(e0, es)) for e0, es in combos for T in temps_scan],
                         t_end=2400, t_skip=1600)
per_scan = per_scan.reshape(len(combos), -1)
n_low = len(temps_scan) - 2
stop_scan = {c: temps_scan[:n_low][np.isfinite(r[:n_low])].min() for c, r in zip(combos, per_scan)}
r45_scan = {c: r[-1] / r[-2] for c, r in zip(combos, per_scan)}

mem_scan = [(c, Tp) for c in combos for Tp in cycle_T]
Tp_scan = np.array([Tp for _, Tp in mem_scan])
stats_scan, _, _ = run_forced(p_ref, [[balance_E(*c)[n] for n in RATE_NAMES] for c, _ in mem_scan],
                              lambda t: np.where(np.mod(t, Tp_scan) < Tp_scan / 2, 45.0, 30.0),
                              t_end=5000, t_skip=4000)
lock_scan = {c: " ".join("○" if is_locked(st, Tp) else "×" for st, (cc, Tp) in zip(stats_scan, mem_scan) if cc == c)
             for c in combos}
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-param-scan
#| tbl-cap: "Oscillation stopping temperatures and entrainment to 30/45 °C cycles (periods: 16, 20, 24, 28, and 32 hours) in the division-of-labor strategy, varying the activation energy $E_0$ of the temperature-insensitive reactions and that of U → T. Experimental results are approximately 19 °C and '× ○ ○ ○ ×'. The rightmost column gives the period ratio at 45 °C versus 30 °C with a U → T activation energy of 70 kJ/mol."
#| tbl-colwidths: [16, 23, 23, 23, 15]
def cell(c):
    st = stop_scan[c]
    st_s = f"≤{temps_scan[0]:.0f} °C" if st <= temps_scan[0] else f"{st:.1f} °C"
    return f"{st_s}  {lock_scan[c]}"
lines = ["| $E_0$ (kJ/mol) | " + " | ".join(f"U → T: {es:.0f} kJ/mol" for es in sens_scan) + " | 45 °C / 30 °C |",
         "|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|"]
for e0 in E0_scan:
    lines.append(f"| {e0:g} | " + " | ".join(cell((e0, es)) for es in sens_scan) + f" | {r45_scan[(e0, 70.0)]:.3f} |")
Markdown("\n".join(lines))
```

Keeping $E_0$ at 10 kJ/mol while lowering the U → T activation energy brings the stopping temperature closer to experiment, but eliminates entrainment to the 28-hour cycle. Entrainment at 28 hours is marginal: it appears only when U → T reaches 70 kJ/mol. Varying $E_0$ as well allows both observations to be matched. For example, $E_0$ = 12.5 kJ/mol and U → T = 50 kJ/mol give a stopping temperature of `{python} f"{stop_scan[(12.5, 50.0)]:.1f}"` °C and an entrainment pattern of "`{python} lock_scan[(12.5, 50.0)]`," both matching experiment. This is fitting two parameters to two observations, however, and does not establish that the model is correct.

If $E_0$ is increased too far, the period starts to lengthen at high temperatures. With U → T at 70 kJ/mol, the period at 45 °C remains almost equal to that at 30 °C for $E_0$ up to 15 kJ/mol, but reaches `{python} f"{r45_scan[(20.0, 70.0)]:.3f}"` times the 30 °C value at 20 kJ/mol. An activation energy of 15 kJ/mol corresponds to a reaction-rate Q~10~ of approximately `{python} f"{q10_rate(15):.1f}"`. For the division-of-labor strategy to work, period-controlling reactions must therefore be about as temperature-insensitive as the KaiC ATPase discussed in Section 2, whose Q~10~ is approximately 1.2 with KaiA and KaiB present [@terauchi2007]. We examine whether this assumption holds in the actual clock in Section 11.

There are other mismatches. Except in the cancellation strategy, period Q~10~ between 25 and 35 °C is close to 1.00, more strongly compensated than the experimental 1.05–1.1. This follows from balancing the ledger exactly to zero at 30 °C. Experimentally, stable rhythms are lost above 45 °C, whereas all models except the cancellation strategy continue oscillating beyond 50 °C. The model does not include processes such as changes to the proteins themselves at high temperature. Finally, its dependence on KaiA concentration goes in the opposite direction from experiment.

```{python}
#| label: kaia-dependence
kaia_list = [1.3, 1.45]
per_ka, _ = period_amp([at_temperature({**p_ref, "KAIA": ka}, T, STRATEGIES["R"]) for ka in kaia_list for T in (25.0, 35.0)],
                       t_end=2400, t_skip=1600)
q10_ka = per_ka.reshape(len(kaia_list), 2)[:, 0] / per_ka.reshape(len(kaia_list), 2)[:, 1]
```

Increasing KaiA from 1.3 to 1.45 µM in the division-of-labor strategy lowers Q~10~ from `{python} f"{q10_ka[0]:.3f}"` to `{python} f"{q10_ka[1]:.3f}"`, shifting it toward overcompensation. Experimentally, increasing KaiA raises Q~10~ and weakens compensation [@itomiwa2020]. The model of Hatakeyama and Kaneko, in which competition for KaiA produces compensation, also predicted this experimental direction [@hatakeyama2012]. The discrepancy may be related to the fact that increasing KaiA lengthens the period in the Rust model, with a control coefficient of `{python} f"{C_all['KAIA']:+.2f}"`. A different KaiABC model that represents KaiA concentration effects in more detail reproduces the dependence of Q~10~ on KaiA concentration [@fu2024].

Within the Rust model, then, neither stopping temperature nor entrainment clearly distinguishes the division-of-labor and coupled strategies. None reproduces the gradual disappearance of amplitude observed experimentally. Even adding amplitude and phase response to period compensation leaves it difficult to identify a unique model design from the experiments. And so far, all activation energies have been chosen by us.

## Building a ledger from measured values {#sec-measured}

What are the activation energies of actual KaiABC reactions? In a recent preprint, Liu and colleagues estimated the rates of individual KaiC phosphorylation and dephosphorylation steps by fitting measurements separately at 20 and 30 °C [@liu2026]. Their supplementary tables list ratios of rates at 30 versus 20 °C for reactions closely corresponding to those in the Rust model.

Liu and colleagues' "KaiA-dependent" rates correspond to the KaiA-bound rates $k^{\mathrm{bound}}$ in @eq-kxy2, and their "baseline" rates correspond to $k^{\mathrm{free}}$. The parameter describing KaiA's effect corresponds to $K_{1/2}$. Their model, however, is based on the Phong model [@phong2013], an extension of the Rust model, and its reference rates differ somewhat. Some tabulated estimates also have large standard errors. For example, the KaiA-bound T → ST and ST → T rates are estimated to fall to less than one fifth upon warming, and the standard error for T → ST at 30 °C exceeds the estimated rate itself. Liu and colleagues selected two well-determined phosphorylation steps and three dephosphorylation steps, incorporating the temperature dependences of these five rates into their model. We follow that choice, assigning temperature dependence to only those five rates and treating the others as temperature-independent. Their model does not include temperature dependence of $K_{1/2}$, so we add that separately for comparison.

```{python}
#| label: measured
# Liu et al. (2026), supplementary Table S1: rate ratios at 30 °C versus 20 °C (KaiA-dependent rates are for KaiA-bound states)
liu_ratio = {"UT_b": 1.60, "TD_b": 0.06, "SD_b": 1.31, "US_b": 1.17, "TU_b": 1.16, "DT_b": 0.20,
             "TU_f": 1.37, "DS_f": 2.60, "SU_f": 5.80}
liu_ratio_K = 1.38                                            # Constant governing the effect of KaiA (K½)
liu_used = ["UT_b", "US_b", "TU_f", "DS_f", "SU_f"]           # Values used in Liu et al.'s model (red in their table)
liu_dissoc = 3.49                                             # Table S2: KaiA-mediated dissociation of the KaiB–KaiC complex

def E_from_fold(fold, T1=20.0, T2=30.0):
    """Activation energy (kJ/mol) for a rate multiplied by fold from T1 to T2."""
    return R_GAS * np.log(fold) / (1 / (T1 + 273.15) - 1 / (T2 + 273.15))

E_all = {n: E_from_fold(liu_ratio[n]) for n in RATE_NAMES}
E_liu = {n: (E_all[n] if n in liu_used else 0.0) for n in RATE_NAMES}
H_liu = E_from_fold(liu_ratio_K)
led_liu = sum(C[n] * E_liu[n] for n in RATE_NAMES)
led_liu_K = led_liu + C_all["KHALF"] * H_liu
aled_liu = sum(CA[n] * E_liu[n] for n in RATE_NAMES)
aled_liu_K = aled_liu + CA_all["KHALF"] * H_liu
q10_from_ledger = lambda L: np.exp(-L * 10 / (R_GAS * (T_REF + 273.15) ** 2))   # Estimate period Q10 from the ledger
E_dissoc = E_from_fold(liu_dissoc)
# Alternative rate selections: adding S→ST, or including all nine rates (including negative activation energies)
led_plus_SD = led_liu + C["SD_b"] * E_all["SD_b"]
led_all9 = sum(C[n] * E_all[n] for n in RATE_NAMES)
led_all9_K = led_all9 + C_all["KHALF"] * H_liu

temps_m = np.arange(15.0, 40.01, 0.5)
cases_m = [(E_liu, 0.0), (E_liu, H_liu)]
per_m, amp_m = period_amp([at_temperature(p_ref, T, E, H) for E, H in cases_m for T in temps_m],
                          t_end=4000, t_skip=2500)
per_m = per_m.reshape(len(cases_m), -1)
amp_m = amp_m.reshape(len(cases_m), -1)
i30_m = np.argmin(abs(temps_m - 30))
i25_m = np.argmin(abs(temps_m - 25))
range_m = [(temps_m[np.isfinite(r)].min(), temps_m[np.isfinite(r)].max()) for r in per_m]
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-liu
#| tbl-cap: "Values from Table S1 of Liu et al. (2026), mapped onto reactions in the Rust model. Ratios compare rates at 30 °C and 20 °C. Control coefficients are from the Rust model at 30 °C. ○ marks values used in Liu et al.'s own model."
#| tbl-colwidths: [26, 14, 18, 14, 16, 12]
lines = ["| Reaction | 30 °C / 20 °C | Activation energy (kJ/mol) | Control coefficient C | Contribution C×E (kJ/mol) | Used |",
         "|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|:--:|"]
for n in RATE_NAMES:
    lines.append(f"| {LABELS[n]} | {liu_ratio[n]:.2f} | {E_all[n]:.0f} | {C[n]:+.2f} | {C[n] * E_all[n]:+.0f} | "
                 f"{'○' if n in liu_used else '—'} |")
lines.append(f"| K½ (constant governing the effect of KaiA) | {liu_ratio_K:.2f} | {H_liu:.0f} | {C_all['KHALF']:+.2f} | "
             f"{C_all['KHALF'] * H_liu:+.0f} | — |")
Markdown("\n".join(lines))
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-measured-ledger
#| fig-cap: "Contributions of the five rates used in Liu et al.'s model to the period ledger (left) and amplitude ledger (right). The bottom row shows the contribution of K½ if it is included."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Figure code"
rows_m = liu_used + ["KHALF"]
lab_m = [LABELS[n] for n in liu_used] + ["K½ (if included)"]
vals_P = [C[n] * E_liu[n] for n in liu_used] + [C_all["KHALF"] * H_liu]
vals_A = [CA[n] * E_liu[n] for n in liu_used] + [CA_all["KHALF"] * H_liu]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, sharey=True)
for ax, vals, title, tot in ((axes[0], vals_P, "Period ledger", led_liu), (axes[1], vals_A, "Amplitude ledger", aled_liu)):
    colors = [ORANGE if v > 0 else BLUE for v in vals]
    bars = ax.barh(lab_m[::-1], vals[::-1], color=colors[::-1], height=0.6)
    bars[0].set_alpha(0.45)
    ax.axvline(0, color=INK2, lw=0.8)
    ax.set_axisbelow(True)
    ax.set_title(f"{title} (sum of 5: {tot:+.0f} kJ/mol)", fontsize=10.5, loc="left")
    ax.set_xlabel("Contribution (kJ/mol)")
    ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

These estimates remain open to debate. Earlier studies reported that KaiC phosphorylation and dephosphorylation rates were largely temperature-independent [@tomita2005; @nakajima2005]. Liu and colleagues argue that those measurements covered too short a time and did not distinguish modification at individual sites. Because S431 dephosphorylates only after T432, they suggest that its temperature dependence becomes apparent only over longer observations. The inputs used here should therefore be regarded as unsettled.

@tbl-liu and @fig-measured-ledger show that the clock's components are indeed temperature-sensitive under these estimates. Two dephosphorylation steps stand out: ST → S without KaiA, at approximately `{python} f"{E_all['DS_f']:.0f}"` kJ/mol, and S → U, at approximately `{python} f"{E_all['SU_f']:.0f}"` kJ/mol. The period ledger does not balance. ST → S also has a large control coefficient, `{python} f"{C['DS_f']:+.2f}"`, so it alone contributes `{python} f"{C['DS_f'] * E_all['DS_f']:+.0f}"` kJ/mol. The five rates sum to `{python} f"{led_liu:+.0f}"` kJ/mol, or `{python} f"{led_liu_K:+.0f}"` kJ/mol with $K_{1/2}$. This value depends strongly on which estimates are included. Adding S → ST, whose rate ratio is 1.31, gives `{python} f"{led_plus_SD:+.0f}"` kJ/mol. Including all nine rates, including the negative activation energies for T → ST and ST → T, gives `{python} f"{led_all9:+.0f}"` kJ/mol, or `{python} f"{led_all9_K:+.0f}"` kJ/mol with $K_{1/2}$. The deficit varies severalfold with the selection, but the ledger is negative in every case. Using the same five rates as Liu and colleagues, the ledger predicts a period Q~10~ of `{python} f"{q10_from_ledger(led_liu):.1f}"`–`{python} f"{q10_from_ledger(led_liu_K):.1f}"`, making the clock even more temperature-sensitive than the all-50-kJ/mol clock of Section 5, whose Q~10~ was about 1.9.

```{python}
#| label: fig-measured-temp
#| fig-cap: "Temperature dependence of period (left) and amplitude (right) in the model using Liu et al.'s measurements, normalized to their values at 30 °C. Points show experiments: periods from Nakajima et al. (2005) and amplitudes from Murayama et al. (2017)."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.9
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Figure code"
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2)
for k, (lab, c) in enumerate((("5 rates", "#5f9de0"), ("5 rates + K½", "#1f5fae"))):
    ax[0].plot(temps_m, per_m[k] / per_m[k, i30_m], color=c, label=lab)
    ax[1].plot(temps_m, amp_m[k] / amp_m[k, i30_m], color=c, label=lab)
ax[0].plot([25, 30, 35], np.array([22, 21, 20]) / 21, "s", color="#0b0b0b", ms=6, label="Nakajima et al. 2005")
ax[0].set(xlim=(15, 40), ylim=(0.5, 4.5), xlabel="Temperature (°C)", ylabel="Period / period at 30 °C")
ax[0].legend(fontsize=8.5)
ax[1].plot(murayama[:, 0], murayama[:, 2] / murayama[-1, 2], "o", color="#0b0b0b", ms=5, label="Murayama et al. 2017")
ax[1].set(xlim=(15, 40), ylim=(-0.05, 2.5), xlabel="Temperature (°C)", ylabel="Amplitude / amplitude at 30 °C")
ax[1].legend(fontsize=8.5, loc="upper right")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Running the model (@fig-measured-temp) confirms the ledger's prediction: the period increases sharply on cooling. At 25 °C, it is `{python} f"{per_m[0, i25_m] / per_m[0, i30_m]:.1f}"` times the 30 °C value, or `{python} f"{per_m[1, i25_m] / per_m[1, i30_m]:.1f}"` times with $K_{1/2}$ included, and oscillations persist only from `{python} f"{range_m[0][0]:.1f}"` to `{python} f"{range_m[0][1]:.1f}"` °C. The amplitude ledger is also negative, `{python} f"{aled_liu:+.0f}"` kJ/mol, so amplitude decreases as temperature rises. Both period and amplitude behave contrary to the experimental observations. Liu and colleagues likewise report that including only the temperature dependences of reaction rates in their model makes the period increase substantially on cooling.

The ledger is therefore missing a large positive contribution. If all reactions accelerate with temperature, only reactions with positive control coefficients—those that lengthen the period when accelerated—can supply it. As noted in Section 3, negative apparent activation energies or changes in equilibrium constants provide other possibilities. The deficit shrinks when all nine rates are included because T → ST combines a negative activation energy with a negative control coefficient, giving a positive contribution. Within the Rust model, S → ST is the principal period-lengthening candidate. But its measured ratio of 1.31 corresponds to only about `{python} f"{E_all['SD_b']:.0f}"` kJ/mol, contributing just `{python} f"{C['SD_b'] * E_all['SD_b']:+.0f}"` kJ/mol when included.

Liu and colleagues identify a candidate for the missing term outside the Rust model: KaiA-mediated dissociation of the KaiB–KaiC complex. According to their supplementary Table S2, this rate increases `{python} f"{liu_dissoc:.2f}"`-fold between 20 and 30 °C, corresponding to an activation energy of approximately `{python} f"{E_dissoc:.0f}"` kJ/mol. They identify this as a reaction of the kind described by Fu and colleagues: one that lengthens the period when accelerated [@liu2026; @fu2024]. A simple division suggests that a period control coefficient of roughly `{python} f"{-led_liu / E_dissoc:.1f}"`–`{python} f"{-led_liu_K / E_dissoc:.1f}"` for this process could fill the deficit. This is not a self-consistent estimate, however. Adding a reaction changes the control coefficients of other reactions so that the summation theorem, @eq-sum, remains satisfied. If the new reaction has a coefficient of +1.2, for instance, the remaining coefficients must sum to −2.2. If that additional negative control falls on temperature-sensitive dephosphorylation, the deficit itself grows. The value 1.1–1.3 must therefore not be treated as a biological estimate. We can say only that the proposed term has the right sign and a plausible order of magnitude. The Rust model compresses formation and dissociation of the KaiB–KaiC complex into the instantaneous relation "S sequesters KaiA," @eq-freeA, so this term is absent by construction. In ledger terms, Liu and colleagues' model becomes compensated only after including the temperature dependence of the KaiA–KaiB switch because this supplies a positive term.^[The same Table S2 also fits an 8.8-fold increase from 20 to 30 °C for complex dissociation without KaiA, implying strong temperature dependence. This conflicts with Simon and colleagues' measurement that dissociation without KaiA is almost temperature-independent [@simon2022]. Liu and colleagues themselves cite that earlier conclusion in their main text. Individual fitted estimates therefore require caution.]

This ledger suggests a possible picture. Temperature-sensitive dephosphorylation, ST → S and S → U, acts to shorten the period, while a temperature-sensitive KaiA–KaiB switch acts to lengthen it; a small number of steps cancel one another. Because the switch also determines amplitude [@liu2026], period compensation and amplitude changes arise from the same mechanism. In the terminology of Section 9, this is a coupled strategy concentrated in a few steps. The strongest support for this picture does not come from our ledger calculation, however. It comes from Liu and colleagues' experiments with a mutant whose phosphorylation state is fixed, KaiC-EE, demonstrating history dependence, or bistability, through KaiA–KaiB antagonism, together with their reproduction of temperature compensation in a model containing that behavior. Our ledger calculation is best viewed as an aid to interpreting those results.

Under this mapping to the Rust model, the division-of-labor assumption—that period-controlling reactions are temperature-insensitive—is also inconsistent with the strongly controlling ST → S reaction having an activation energy of about `{python} f"{E_all['DS_f']:.0f}"` kJ/mol. But these control coefficients belong to the Rust model. Because it lacks ATPase, it may concentrate period control in ST → S. In the mutants studied by Furuike and colleagues, ATPase temperature dependence and clock-frequency temperature dependence change together [@furuike2022], suggesting that a substantial fraction of period control in the actual clock resides in ATPase. If so, the ST → S control coefficient, and hence the ledger deficit, would be smaller.

This inference rests on several assumptions. We have used control coefficients from the Rust model. The measurements cover only two temperatures, 20 and 30 °C, and some fitted estimates are poorly constrained. The switch's control coefficient cannot be calculated in the Rust model. An unbalanced ledger can reflect not only missing reactions but also differences in how models distribute control, how processes are grouped into reactions, and uncertainty in the estimated values. Within this mapping, we can conclude that the measured components alone do not reproduce compensation, that the missing contribution's sign agrees with the switch described by Liu and colleagues, and that this motivates testing a model with an explicit switch. Even with these limits, the ledger makes concrete what should be investigated next.

## Discussion: viewing the actual clock through its ledgers {#sec-discussion}

We have organized ways of balancing the period ledger into three strategies: uniformly insensitive, coupled, and division of labor. Again, these categories are a conceptual aid; the same mechanism may appear in different categories depending on the level at which it is examined. With that in mind, let us read recent findings in the language of ledgers.

First is the view that KaiC ATPase sets the period. Mutants with disrupted ATPase temperature compensation also show disrupted compensation of clock frequency in the same direction [@furuike2022]. A preprint proposes a mechanism for compensation of ATPase itself [@itomiwa2026]: ADP release determines the ATPase rate, and warming shifts KaiC toward the ADP-bound state, offsetting the acceleration of hydrolysis. This is cancellation within a molecule, but from the whole clock's perspective it is a temperature-insensitive component that determines the period. The same preprint reports that ATPase rhythm amplitude is temperature-sensitive, with Q~10~ ≈ 2.1. A temperature-insensitive period-setting component, with temperature sensitivity expressed through amplitude, resembles the division-of-labor strategy. As stressed in Section 7, it differs from a uniformly insensitive strategy in which every reaction is insensitive. The ATPase–period relationship is not simple, however. Changing pH can shift the period from approximately 15 to 36 hours while ATPase activity changes by only about 15%, with temperature compensation preserved [@itomiwa2025]. Furthermore, as discussed in Section 11, phosphorylation and dephosphorylation steps are themselves temperature-sensitive and require compensation somewhere in addition to ATPase. The report that compensation of KaiC-alone ATPase breaks down between 4 and 20 °C, with Q~10~ = 1.39 [@itomiwa2026], also raises the question of whether this is related to the clock stopping near 19 °C.

A second view regards amplitude changes themselves as part of compensation, corresponding to the coupled strategy. Ruoff and colleagues argued that a compensated oscillator must traverse a larger orbit as temperature rises to maintain the same period [@ruoff2003]. Kurosawa and colleagues likewise derived from mathematical models a relationship in which maintaining period requires amplitude to increase with temperature [@kurosawa2017]. Liu and colleagues' switch is a KaiABC example, and the measured-value ledger in Section 11 was consistent with this picture. A model incorporating the relationship between KaiC's hexameric structure and its reactions also proposes that warming increases amplitude and period in a way that offsets reaction acceleration [@sasai2022]. Temperature-dependent conformational changes in KaiB itself have also been discussed as contributors to compensation [@zhang2024]. Proteins such as KaiB that interconvert between two folds often show partial unfolding of one fold at low temperature, and this sensitivity has been proposed as an adaptation to environmental temperature [@liwang2025].

The views of François and colleagues and of Kidd and colleagues, introduced in Section 9, are closer to division of labor. In *Drosophila*, both the mean abundance and oscillation amplitude of the clock protein TIM rise with temperature; amplitude approximately doubles between 18 and 29 °C. Kidd and colleagues report unchanged waveform and phase relationships between components, interpreting this as evidence for a temperature-insensitive core oscillator coupled to a dedicated temperature-sensing pathway [@kidd2015]. A reanalysis of the same data, however, reports greater waveform distortion at higher temperature [@gibo2025].

These views are not mutually exclusive. Components compensated within a molecule, such as ATPase, can coexist in the same clock with components that affect both period and amplitude, such as a switch. They may even be different aspects of the same molecular process. According to Ito-Miwa and colleagues' preprint, within the KaiB–KaiC complex, KaiA accelerates ADP-to-ATP exchange in KaiC's CI domain, stimulating CI ATPase activity and promoting KaiB dissociation [@itomiwa2026]. KaiA-mediated complex dissociation, the candidate missing positive term in Section 11, may thus be connected to ATPase nucleotide state through a single process. In *Neurospora*, temperature-dependent changes in clock-protein abundance have been proposed to mediate temperature-induced phase shifts [@liu1998]. Earlier modeling also showed that a temperature-compensated oscillator can become damped at low temperature and entrain to temperature cycles of only about 1 °C [@ruoff1996].

Some questions remain. Fu and colleagues showed that compensation through period-lengthening reactions works more readily far from a bifurcation [@fu2024]. Yet, as discussed in Section 9, the in vitro clock appears to operate relatively near a Hopf bifurcation even over 20–30 °C. Approximate proportionality of amplitude squared to temperature alone does not establish that it is too close for the mechanism of Fu and colleagues to operate, and their argument does not prohibit compensation near a bifurcation. How individual reaction contributions change in that regime remains insufficiently explained by this model.

Finally, we should keep the model's limitations in view. The Rust model contains neither KaiC ATPase nor hexameric structure, KaiB conformational changes, or the bistability identified by Liu and colleagues. Its amplitude control coefficients depend strongly on the sharp KaiA sequestration switch in @eq-freeA, making the amplitude ledger's values specific to this model. The role of U → T as a temperature sensor is likewise a model-specific result. In living cells, transcription–translation feedback and output pathways transmitting clock information to gene expression are also coupled to the clock [@chavan2021]. The ledger perspective nevertheless applies beyond these model details. Calculating period, amplitude, and phase-response sensitivities and weighting them by activation energies provides a common measure for comparing which reactions maintain the clock's pace and which sense temperature.

## Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

Let us return to the three properties introduced in Section 1. Temperature compensation could be expressed as a balanced period ledger, @eq-tc. Stopping at low temperature was connected to the amplitude ledger in @eq-dlnA, and entrainment to temperature cycles to the phase-response ledger in @eq-gamma. In both the amplitude and phase-response ledgers, deviations from the mean activation energy are what matter. A temperature-dependent amplitude therefore means that temperature does more than uniformly fast-forward the system; and a clock with identical activation energies cannot entrain to temperature cycles, however strongly its rate responds to temperature.

The central point of this article is that period compensation alone does not identify its mechanism. There are many ways to make the period ledger zero. As Sections 9 and 10 showed, even amplitude and phase response may not uniquely identify a model's design. But placing period, amplitude, phase response, and measured temperature dependences of individual reactions in the same ledger can narrow down the processes missing from a model and turn them into concrete, testable hypotheses.

Section 11 attempted exactly that. Inserting measured reaction temperature dependences into the ledger showed that the phosphorylation and dephosphorylation components alone did not balance it or reproduce compensation. The missing contribution had to be positive, on the period-lengthening side, consistent with the properties of KaiA-mediated dissociation of the KaiB–KaiC complex: a temperature-sensitive switch. This is a hypothesis to test in a model that includes the switch explicitly. Our opening question was why a clock can be insensitive to temperature when its components are sensitive. In ledger terms, there is no contradiction: the contributions of temperature-sensitive components can cancel. Constructing the ledger gives us a concrete way to look for the compensating partner.

A clock made from three proteins in a test tube offers a rare setting in which to address these questions in both molecular and mathematical terms. All the code is included on this page. Try replacing the measured values or changing which reactions are temperature-sensitive, and build your own ledger.
